name: Security Engineering
experience: 3 years of security experience + LLM application experience
purpose: This exam verifies that candidates can identify threats unique to LLM applications and agents, and defend, detect, and validate using security features and recommendations from the three providers.
guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam verifies that candidates can identify threats unique to LLM applications and agents, and defend, detect, and validate using security features and recommendations from the three providers.

**Objectives**

- Model threats to LLM and agent systems (direct and indirect prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse)
- Apply input/output filtering, system prompt protection, and jailbreak mitigation
- Limit the impact of agents through least-privilege tools, approval steps, and sandboxes
- Minimize sensitive information exposure through data retention and logging settings
- Validate defenses through red teaming and adversarial evaluation, detect abuse, and respond to incidents

### 2. Target candidates

- Application security engineers, security architects, red team specialists

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- Three years of security experience and an understanding of LLM application architecture (ADA level) are recommended.

### 3. Content domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. LLM threat modeling | 15% |
| 2. Prompt injection and jailbreak defense | 22% |
| 3. Agent and tool security | 20% |
| 4. Data protection | 15% |
| 5. Red teaming and safety evaluation | 18% |
| 6. Detection and response | 10% |

**Domain 1: LLM threat modeling**

- Knowledge: Attack surfaces (user input, retrieved documents, web pages, tool results, MCP servers), risk categories in the Secure AI Framework (SAIF)
- Skills: Identify trust boundaries and the highest-risk paths from a system architecture diagram

**Domain 2: Prompt injection and jailbreak defense**

- Knowledge: Direct/indirect injection, types of jailbreak techniques, system prompt leakage, moderation APIs, prompt/response filtering services, safety settings
- Skills: Choose the most effective combination of defense layers (input inspection, context separation, output inspection, permission restrictions) for a given threat

**Domain 3: Agent and tool security**

- Knowledge: Least-privilege tool design, tool approval steps, permission modes, pre-execution checks using hooks, sandboxes, risks of computer-use tools, trust issues with remote MCP servers
- Skills: Separate permissions so that an agent reading external content cannot abuse write privileges

**Domain 4: Data protection**

- Knowledge: API data retention periods across the three providers, zero-retention options, retention for abuse monitoring, data captured in logs, file store lifetimes
- Skills: Choose the configuration with the smallest exposure footprint for systems handling personal information

**Domain 5: Red teaming and safety evaluation**

- Knowledge: Red team planning (scope, attack scenarios, records), adversarial evaluation sets, automated attack generation, metrics for measuring defense effectiveness
- Skills: Adjust defense strength by balancing refusal rates and attack success rates

**Domain 6: Detection and response**

- Knowledge: Abuse monitoring, anomalous usage patterns, audit logs, response to key exposure
- Skills: Determine the sequence of actions that most quickly limits the impact of an injection incident

### 4. Official documentation

**OpenAI**

- [Safety best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices) · [Red teaming](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/red-teaming) · [Moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation)
- [Guardrails and approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/guardrails-approvals) · [Agents SDK guardrails](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/)
- [MCP servers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp) · [Data controls in the OpenAI platform](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data)

**Anthropic**

questions.title: Choosing the first defense layer for an agent that reads incoming email
questions.prompt:
A team operating an internal email assistant with the Claude API is revisiting its threat model. At an authenticated employee's request, the agent searches the inbox with read-only tools and summarizes messages. Currently, the backend appends retrieved email bodies to the employee's request and sends them as user-turn text. The red team identifies external senders hiding agent-targeted instructions in email bodies as the greatest risk. The constraints are:

- Employees are internal staff authenticated through SSO; the security team does not consider employee accounts to be attackers.
- Summary responses already consume most of the latency budget (p95 4 seconds), so **the number of model calls per request cannot increase**.
- If an email contains instructions aimed at the agent, **the employee must be informed** so the security team can use that information in a phishing report.

Which is the **most appropriate first defense layer** to implement this quarter?

options.text: Move email bodies into `tool_result`, classify each tool result for suspected injection with Claude Haiku 5.5, return an error instead of the original text if suspicious, and display the attempt to the employee.

Move email bodies into `tool_result` and label their source, but use backend regular expressions to find known injection patterns such as "ignore previous instructions" and remove those sentences before forwarding them.

Remove email bodies from user text and pass them as JSON-wrapped `tool_result`, label them as emails from unknown senders, and state in the system prompt that they are data only and that any instructions found must be reported to the employee.

First inspect the employee request with a Claude Haiku 5.5 harmlessness screen and rate-limit accounts that repeatedly trigger the same refusal, filtering attempts to misuse the email assistant at the front of the conversation.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic distinguishes jailbreaks/direct injection, where the user is the attacker, from indirect injection, where the user is trusted but third-party content such as email, documents, or tool results contains attack instructions. Structural defenses for indirect injection include placing untrusted content only in 'tool_result' (not system prompts or ordinary user text blocks), identifying its source, wrapping it in JSON to clarify boundaries, and stating in the system prompt that the content cannot change the goal and that embedded instructions must be reported to the user rather than followed. The documentation also proposes inspecting tool results with a Haiku 5.5 classifier, but that layer adds a model call. The decisive evidence is [employees are not attackers], [call count cannot increase], and [notify employees about instructions], which eliminate {{option:D}}, {{option:A}}, and {{option:B}} respectively.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: This is a documented classifier layer and satisfies notification, but classifying every tool result adds calls and violates the latency constraint. It is a next layer to add on top of {{option:C}} when call budget becomes available.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The documentation mentions applying input-validation patterns to tool results, but silently deleting instructions prevents employees and security staff from learning about the attempt. Expressions absent from the pattern list also pass through.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It establishes a structural trust boundary without additional calls and uses a prompt policy to report detected instructions. The tradeoff is residual reliance on model judgment without a separate detection layer, so red-team tests with injected emails are needed.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, applies to a different situation)**: Harmlessness screening and repeat-offender measures address malicious users. Here attack instructions arrive in email bodies, not employee requests; the screen call also violates latency constraints.

Additional point: The same documentation recommends placing your own instructions in the user turn after 'tool_result', rather than mixing them into tool results. Concatenating requests and email bodies into a single text block, as the current implementation does, erases that boundary.

**References**: [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Indirect prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks)

questions.title: Prioritizing SAIF controls for a model consumer team
questions.prompt:
A customer-support agent followed instructions hidden in a ticket, used a CRM tool to retrieve another customer's contact details without the support representative requesting them, included those details in its answer, and even executed a refund tool. A security architect records three risks using Google SAIF (Secure AI Framework): Prompt Injection, Sensitive Data Disclosure, and Rogue Actions. The architect must now select one control package for the next quarter.

- The team is a **model consumer** using an external model through an API; it does not train or tune models.
- Assuming injection cannot be eliminated completely, its highest priority is **limiting the blast radius**.
- The package must include **at least one SAIF-mapped control for each of the three recorded risks**.

Which package is **most appropriate** under SAIF's risk-control mapping?

options.text: Agent Permissions · Agent User Control · Agent Observability · Output Validation and Sanitization
Input Validation and Sanitization · Adversarial Training and Testing · Output Validation and Sanitization
Privacy Enhancing Technologies · User Data Management · Training Data Management
Application Access Management · Agent Permissions · Agent Observability

questions.explanation:
SAIF assigns responsibility for Rogue Actions (unintended agent behavior) to model consumers and maps Agent Permissions, Agent User Control, Agent Observability, and Output Validation and Sanitization to this risk. All four also map to Sensitive Data Disclosure (alongside Privacy Enhancing Technologies and User Data Management). Prompt Injection maps to Input Validation and Sanitization, Adversarial Training and Testing, and Output Validation and Sanitization. The decisive evidence is [prioritize limiting the blast radius] and [at least one control for each risk]. Only {{option:A}} directly reduces impact through agent permissions, user control, and observability while covering all three risks through Output Validation.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: All four controls map to Rogue Actions and Sensitive Data Disclosure; Output Validation and Sanitization also maps to Prompt Injection. Reduced permissions and user confirmation directly limit impact.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Output Validation technically covers all three risks, but the package focuses on input validation and adversarial testing to prevent injection itself. It lacks agent controls that reduce actions and data access after injection succeeds, violating the top priority.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, applies to a different situation)**: Training Data Management concerns training data and does not apply to a consumer team that does not train models. The package contains no controls mapped to Prompt Injection or Rogue Actions.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Application Access Management maps to Denial of ML Service and Model Reverse Engineering. The package has no control mapped to Prompt Injection and therefore violates the third condition.

Additional point: SAIF treats Assurance and Governance controls as common to all risks and all actors, addressing them separately from risk-specific mappings.

**References**: [SAIF › Risks](https://saif.google/secure-ai-framework/risks) · [SAIF › Controls](https://saif.google/secure-ai-framework/controls)

questions.title: Exfiltration paths in a research agent with web fetching
questions.prompt:
Consultancy Nuri Insight is building a research agent with the Claude API. Its tools are:

- Server tool `web_fetch`: researches the public web broadly.
- Client tool `search_internal`: searches confidential internal reports and returns results.
- Client tool `save_note`: saves notes written by Claude and **returns the received note text unchanged as confirmation**.

A threat-model review identified a path in which an indirect injection on a researched web page could induce the agent to send an external fetch request containing confidential information. Mitigations implemented this quarter must satisfy these constraints:

- Research targets vary by industry, so **a domain list cannot be predetermined**.
- Draft reports must **cross-reference web sources and internal figures within the same conversation**.
- Saving research notes is a core consultant workflow and **cannot be removed**. Changing tool-result formats is possible, but no new services or infrastructure may be built.

Choose **two appropriate mitigations** within these constraints.

options.text: Change `save_note` to return only a storage ID instead of the received text, eliminating the path that returns Claude-written text through a tool result as an allowed fetch source. Keep note saving itself.

Split research into web-research and internal-search calls, withholding `search_internal` from calls with `web_fetch`. Have consultants manually combine the results into drafts, preventing confidential content from entering fetch requests.
Restrict `allowed_domains` to several dozen trusted news and government sites so outbound requests reach only listed domains.

Use `max_uses` to cap fetches per request, reducing the number of outbound requests, and register the residual risk of untrusted web content and confidential data sharing a conversation for regular threat-model review.
Disable `save_note` and include research notes only in the final response, eliminating the tool-result path that echoes Claude-written text.

questions.explanation:
The web-fetch documentation warns that enabling the tool where untrusted inputs and sensitive data coexist creates exfiltration risks with residual exposure. It lists disabling the tool, `max_uses`, and `allowed_domains` as mitigations. URL validation allows fetching only URLs appearing in user messages, client-tool results (including results echoing Claude's own text), or earlier web-search/fetch results. The decisive clues are [no predetermined domain list], [cross-references in one conversation], [retain notes without new infrastructure], and the `save_note` return format. These constraints respectively eliminate {{option:C}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:E}}, leaving {{option:A}} and {{option:D}}, each with tradeoffs.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Closes the route by which a model-constructed URL becomes fetchable through `save_note`, while preserving note storage. The confirmation UI must show an ID instead of the original text; other allowed sources, such as URLs in user messages or internal search results, remain possible.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Removes this exfiltration route within a call but violates cross-referencing web and internal data within the same conversation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Greatly reduces exposure but violates the inability to predefine an industry-dependent research scope.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Uses another documented mitigation when domains cannot be restricted and explicitly manages the documented residual risk. The default imposes no usage cap. Small leaks remain possible within the cap, and a low cap limits research depth.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Closes the same route but removes note saving, violating the third constraint. {{option:A}} closes it without losing the feature.

Also note: The tool rejects URLs containing credential-like values unless those values appear in system-prompt or user-message text. Credentials appearing only in tool results do not qualify for the exception.

**References**: [Web fetch tool › URL validation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-fetch-tool) · [Web fetch tool › Max uses](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-fetch-tool)

questions.title: Improving image moderation when illicit-item scores are always zero
questions.prompt:
A secondhand marketplace team sends only listing photos to the OpenAI Moderation API ('omni-moderation-latest'). Even test photos of illegal items always receive an 'illicit' score of 0, while 'violence' scores vary by image. The improvement requirements are:

- Inspection costs **must not increase**. The team currently uses only a free endpoint.
- When blocking a listing, the seller notice must identify **whether the decision was based on the photo or description text**, for handling appeals.
- Improve the rate of filtering illegal-item listings.

Which improvement is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Assume image scores are suppressed and lower the custom `illicit` threshold to around 0.01 so even very low scores trigger blocking.
Send listing photos to a GPT vision model with a classification prompt containing prohibited items, directly judging illegal goods from the photos.
Include title and description text in the same request input array as the photo, block listings when `flagged` is true, and give sellers the generic reason "violation of operating policy."
Include title and description text in the same request as the photo, use `category_applied_input_types` to identify the input types to which category scores apply, and include them in seller notices.

questions.explanation:
'omni-moderation-latest' accepts text and images, but supported input types differ by category. Self-harm categories, 'sexual', 'violence', and 'violence/graphic' support both; categories such as 'illicit', 'harassment', and 'hate' support text only and score 0 for image-only input. The response field 'category_applied_input_types' identifies the input types to which each category score applies. Text and images can share a request input array, and the endpoint is free. The decisive evidence is [no cost increase], [identify supporting input types], and [improve illegal-item detection], which eliminate {{option:B}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:A}} respectively.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, applies to a different situation)**: Threshold recalibration after model upgrades is a real operational task, but these zeros result from an unsupported input type; lowering thresholds detects nothing.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It can work, but introduces generative-model charges and violates the first condition.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Adding text enables 'illicit' detection but discards the requirement to disclose the supporting input type.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A single free endpoint call activates text-only categories and provides input-type information for notices. The tradeoff is that 'illicit' still judges text only: benign descriptions paired with prohibited-item photos can still pass. Another layer, such as sample review, must address that residual risk.

Additional point: Categories supporting both inputs, such as 'violence', can list both text and image as applied types. In that case, disclose both instead of attributing the decision to just one.

**References**: [Moderation › Classify standalone inputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation) · [Safety best practices › Use the free Moderation API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.title: Prioritizing system-prompt leakage mitigations
questions.prompt:
An analytics service using Claude Sonnet 5.5 includes internal formulas in its system prompt and is concerned about users extracting them. Some formulas must be used at each calculation step and cannot be removed. Requirements:

- Reduce leakage risk while **minimizing answer-quality degradation**.
- Display answers through **uninterrupted streaming**.
- Implement within this sprint, with **no new tools or services**.

According to Anthropic's guidance, **which approach should be implemented first**?

options.text: Add as many scenario-specific prohibition rules and refusal examples as possible to the system prompt, retaining streaming.
Keep streaming output while asynchronously checking the same output with keywords, regular expressions, and a lightweight model to alert on leakage; remove unnecessary formulas.
Buffer the entire response and display it only after keyword, regular-expression, and lightweight-model checks pass, blocking flagged responses and removing formulas unnecessary for calculations.
Move formulas into an internal calculation-function tool so the model sends inputs and receives results without seeing formulas; retain streaming.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's prompt-leak guidance states that no approach is foolproof and recommends leakage-prevention techniques only when necessary. Complex prompts can harm other task performance, so monitoring techniques such as output screening and postprocessing should be tried first, and unnecessary confidential information should be omitted. The documentation does not specify whether screening must precede display or run asynchronously; the scenario's constraints decide this. Key clues are [minimize quality degradation], [uninterrupted streaming], and [no new tool development].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Increases prompt complexity and the performance risk the documentation warns about.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Starts with monitoring, removes unnecessary formulas, and preserves streaming. The tradeoff is that asynchronous checks detect leakage after display rather than preventing it; essential formulas remain in the prompt.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Directly blocks leakage at response level, but leaves the screen blank until the entire response is collected, violating streaming.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Most strongly removes formulas from context but requires new tool development and extra call round trips, violating the third constraint. Repeated tool-result queries may still allow reverse-engineering formulas.

Also note: The documentation recommends periodic audits of prompts and outputs.

**References**: [Reduce prompt leak › Before you try to reduce prompt leak](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak) · [Reduce prompt leak › Strategies to reduce prompt leak](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak)

questions.title: Layered jailbreak and direct-injection defenses for an anonymous chatbot
questions.prompt:
Onbit Pharmacy operates a public web chatbot using Claude Sonnet 5.5 under these conditions:

- Anyone can use it without signing in; sessions are distinguished only by cookies. Its privacy policy **prohibits login or phone-number collection**. Users may be attackers. The chatbot reads no tools or external documents, only user messages.
- Dosage, overdose symptoms, and drug interactions are core topics. Overdose questions are directly connected to emergency guidance, so **false blocking or refusal of legitimate questions is costly**.
- Added latency must be limited to roughly one lightweight-model call.
- Operations can review **about 50 blocked or flagged cases daily**.

Choose **two defense layers to combine** against jailbreaks and direct injection.

options.text: Use a static keyword list to block inputs mentioning drug names, dosage units, or "overdose" before they reach the model, and place blocked cases in the operations review queue.
Add a Claude Haiku 5.5 harmlessness screen that returns a structured boolean indicating a service-policy violation; also treat refusal by the screening call as a violation, block it, and log it.
Place user messages in `tool_result` blocks labeled "input of unknown origin" so Claude treats requests as untrusted data, and instruct it not to follow instructions inside them.
Add Google Cloud Model Armor prompt-injection and jailbreak filtering at Low and above confidence with Inspect and block, blocking even minor indicators and alerting operations.
Track sessions that repeatedly trigger refusals, warn them and then rate-limit or block them, and periodically analyze outputs to refine prompts and screening.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic recommends harmlessness screening (Haiku 5.5 with structured outputs, treating screening refusals as harmful), input validation, prompt engineering, repeat-offender responses, and ongoing monitoring for jailbreaks/direct injection where the user is the attacker. It recommends chaining these layers. Its example screen checks specific service policies rather than generic harmfulness. The decisive clues are [anonymous potentially malicious users], [cost of false blocking], [latency limit], and [50 reviews per day]. Reducing false positives and preventing attacks pull in different directions; the correct combination is not perfect.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Documented input validation filters known injection patterns, not topic words. It blocks many core questions, violating both false-positive and review-volume limits.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: A lightweight screen fits the latency budget, and service-specific criteria reduce excessive filtering of legitimate risky-topic questions. It adds one call's latency; sensitive legitimate questions refused by the screen are still blocked.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: `tool_result` placement mitigates indirect injection in third-party content read for a trusted user. Here there is no third-party content; demoting the user's request to data disrupts legitimate handling and violates the false-blocking constraint.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Model Armor documents Low and above as having the most false positives, violating false-blocking and daily review limits.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Targets persistent attackers without increasing false blocking on each individual request, while monitoring enables ongoing improvement. Cookie sessions can easily be replaced to evade this defense, and it does not block the first attempt.

Also note: Treating screen refusals as violations can catch legitimate sensitive questions. After rollout, separately measure false-positive rates on a legitimate-question set and check whether daily blocked cases exceed review capacity.

**References**: [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Advanced: Chain safeguards](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Model Armor overview › Model Armor confidence levels](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview)

questions.title: Redesigning blocking after a model change increases harassing replies
questions.prompt:
A team automatically replying to community comments with the Gemini API changes only the model to Gemini 3, with almost no code changes. The code specifies no safety settings. After the change:

- Sample reviews show noticeably more harassing replies that retaliate against provocative comments.
- The app always resends a request once when the response body is empty, but some requests remain empty on retry and only increase cost.

Requirements:

- The community has many rough jokes among friends, so **minimize false blocking of legitimate comments**.
- Before launch, verify that **severe replies assessed as low-probability risks**, such as subtly worded threats, are not being sent.
- Retry **only when the response is blocked**; send comments with blocked input to human review.

What is the **most appropriate action**?

options.text: Set harassment to the strictest threshold, blocking low probability and above so filters catch subtle threats, and send every empty response to human review without retrying.
Set harassment to block only high probability, and when retrying an empty response, add an instruction to respond politely instead of sending the same request.
Set harassment to block only high probability, route prompt-block reasons to human review and safety response finish reasons to retries, and separately test a set containing subtle threats.

Set harassment to block only high probability and handle prompt and response blocking separately, but omit separate tests because severe threats also receive high probability and the filter setting is sufficient.

questions.explanation:
According to Gemini API documentation, adjustable safety filters are off for Gemini 2.5 and 3 when thresholds are unspecified. Changing only the model without configuring settings explains the increase in harassing replies. Blocking is based on probability, not severity; low-probability text may still describe severe harm, so the documentation recommends testing the appropriate blocking level for the use case. `promptFeedback.blockReason` indicates a blocked prompt, while a blocked response has `finishReason` of `SAFETY`; blocked content is not returned. The decisive evidence is [minimize false blocking], [check low-probability/high-severity replies], and [retry response blocking only], which eliminate {{option:A}}, {{option:D}}, and {{option:B}} respectively.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Blocking low-probability content catches many rough jokes, violating the first condition. It also fails to distinguish blocked input from blocked output, missing the third.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The threshold fits, but it never determines whether empty output resulted from input or response blocking. Blocked input remains the same even after changing the instruction, so it can stay blocked and never enters the review queue.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Explicit settings address the default-off cause, the two blocking signals separate processing paths, and tests cover gaps in probability-based filters. The tradeoff is time to create and review a test set before release.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The documentation separates probability from severity and explains that low-probability text can be severe. Settings alone cannot satisfy the second requirement.

Additional point: Baseline protections against core harms such as child-safety violations always block regardless of settings and cannot be adjusted. Less restrictive settings may be subject to review under the terms of service.

**References**: [Safety settings › Safety filtering per request](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/safety-settings) · [Safety settings › Safety feedback](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/safety-settings)

questions.title: Designing Claude Code sandboxing around approval fatigue and blast radius
questions.prompt:
A platform-security team plans to deploy Claude Code to 300 developers. Requirements:

- Reduce approval prompts for shell commands such as builds and tests to protect **developer productivity**.
- Even if instructions hidden in repository documents manipulate commands, **credentials such as `~/.aws/credentials` and `~/.ssh` must not be read or exfiltrated**.
- Shell-command networking must reach **approved hosts only**, such as the internal package registry.
- Repository-level `.claude/settings.json` files **must not broaden policy**.
- An 80-person integration-test team needs `docker compose up` daily, but `docker` does not work inside the sandbox.

According to Claude Code documentation, **which configuration is most appropriate**?

options.text: Enable sandboxing through managed settings with `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` and `failIfUnavailable`, deny both paths through `sandbox.credentials`, and restrict approved hosts with `allowManagedDomainsOnly`. In the same managed settings, add only `docker compose *` to `excludedCommands` and use auto-allow mode.

Enable sandboxing through managed settings with `failIfUnavailable`, deny both paths through `sandbox.credentials`, and put approved hosts in `allowedDomains`, without restricting retries. Let the Docker team add `docker compose *` to `excludedCommands` in each repository's `.claude/settings.json`; run other commands in auto-allow mode without approval.

Deploy managed allow rules such as `Bash(npm *)`, `Bash(make *)`, and `Bash(docker compose *)`, plus `Read` deny rules for both paths, to reduce prompts; leave sandboxing disabled to avoid compatibility issues.

Apply managed locks (`allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, `failIfUnavailable`, credentials deny, and `allowManagedDomainsOnly`), add `docker compose *` to `excludedCommands`, but disable auto-allow and use normal permission mode so developers approve every command individually.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code sandboxing imposes OS-level filesystem and network boundaries on shell commands. Auto-allow mode runs commands within those boundaries without approval. The default read policy allows most paths, including `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws/credentials`, so they must be explicitly blocked with `sandbox.credentials`. Managed `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` makes sandboxing administrator-required and prevents repository settings from broadening policy, including `excludedCommands`; the Docker exception must therefore be managed. `allowManagedDomainsOnly` permits only managed domains. Key clues are [fewer prompts], [credential protection], [approved hosts only], [no repository policy expansion], and [Docker Compose required].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Boundaries replace approvals, reducing prompts; credential denial, locked domains, and blocked retries constrain manipulated commands. The tradeoff is that `docker compose` runs outside filesystem/network isolation, without credential protection or domain restrictions, and retains normal permission-flow prompts. Narrowing the exception to `docker compose *` reduces this exposure.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Although sandboxing and credential denial are present, unrestricted retries mean sandboxing is not administrator-required. Repository settings can move commands outside it, violating the fourth condition.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Permission rules inspect command strings before execution; they cannot stop an allowed command from doing more than its name suggests. Without sandboxing, shell networking is unrestricted, violating the third condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Its locks and Docker exception match {{option:A}} and are most conservative, but normal permission mode also requires approvals for sandboxed commands, violating the first condition.

Also note: The sandbox wraps shell commands only. Built-in tools such as Read and WebFetch, hooks, and local MCP servers run outside it and need separate permission rules. Sandboxing does not work on native Windows, so `failIfUnavailable` prevents Claude Code from starting there.

questions.title: Guardrails that block side effects across agent handoffs
questions.prompt:
An order-support system built with the OpenAI Agents SDK sends the first input to a triage agent, which may hand off to a refund specialist. The specialist uses internal function tools `get_order` and `issue_refund`. The triage agent has an input guardrail calling an injection/jailbreak classifier with default settings. Red-team tests show that the tripwire fired correctly, but some runs consumed tokens and called tools before it fired. Requirements:

- Malicious inputs must cause **no tool side effects**, and **additional latency is acceptable**.
- Inspect arguments to `issue_refund` **on every call, regardless of the calling agent**.

**Which configuration is most appropriate?**

options.text: Set the triage input guardrail to `run_in_parallel=False`, and instruct the refund specialist to check arguments itself before calling `issue_refund`.
Keep the triage input guardrail in default parallel mode, and attach a tool-input guardrail to `issue_refund` to inspect refund arguments on every call.

Set the triage input guardrail to `run_in_parallel=False`, and attach an output guardrail to the refund specialist producing the final response, triggering a tripwire if the response includes an executed refund.
Set the triage input guardrail to `run_in_parallel=False`, and attach a tool-input guardrail to `issue_refund` to inspect refund arguments on every call.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK input guardrails run in parallel with the agent by default, minimizing latency but allowing token consumption and tool execution before a tripwire fires. Blocking execution with `run_in_parallel=False` starts the agent only after the guardrail finishes, so a tripwire prevents agent token consumption and tools. Input guardrails run only on the first agent, and output guardrails only on the agent producing final output; tool guardrails are recommended for inspecting function calls after handoffs. Key clues are [no side effects, latency acceptable] and [every call regardless of agent].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Blocking meets the first requirement, but an instruction relies on model compliance rather than enforcing every-call inspection, violating the second.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Every-call argument inspection is correct, but parallel execution permits token consumption and tools before the tripwire, violating the first requirement. Its latency is lowest.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Blocking is correct, but output guardrails run after the agent finishes. Completed tool calls and results remain even if a tripwire fires; the refund has already happened, and this is not every-call inspection.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Blocking prevents malicious-input side effects, and tool guardrails inspect every call regardless of handoff path. Every request must await the guardrail decision, delaying the initial response.

Also note: Tool guardrails do not apply to hosted tools such as `HostedMCPTool`. For tools requiring approval, tool-input guardrails normally run after approval immediately before execution; `ToolExecutionConfig(pre_approval_tool_input_guardrails=True)` can also run them before requesting approval.

**References**: [Agents SDK › Guardrails](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/)

| 2–{{option:f}} | Nobody is available to confirm instructions, so classifier-driven confirmation stops work. Isolation and allowlisting are already present; disabling the classifier as documented addresses this case. Option {{option:a}} cannot work without a human. |
| 3–{{option:d}} | The documentation warns that using computer use with login-required apps increases injection impact and advises against providing sensitive data such as login credentials. |

questions.title: Trust boundaries when a ZDR organization connects a third-party remote MCP server
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Legal uses the Claude API in an organization with an Anthropic ZDR agreement. It wants to query case information through a remote MCP server operated by an external case-management vendor. The server exposes dozens of read, update, and delete tools; once or twice monthly, the vendor adds tools or changes descriptions/input schemas. Constraints:

- Client contracts prohibit storing case information at Anthropic **outside the ZDR agreement's scope**.
- Tool descriptions are also model-influencing inputs, so expose **only definitions reviewed by security**. Review takes three business days.
- The feature is **read-only**; updates/deletions remain in the existing case-management UI.
- The platform team has two people, so **fewer self-operated components are preferable**, subordinate to the first three requirements.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Connect with the Messages API MCP connector, disable all tools through `default_config`, enable only reviewed read tools, and pin the tool list with the `mcp-client-2026-09-15` beta.

Have a backend MCP client connect to the vendor and expose only reviewed read tools as fixed-definition client tools to the Messages API; update definitions after re-review when the vendor changes tools.
Have a backend MCP client retrieve the vendor's tool list on every request, convert it with SDK helpers, and pass only read tools whose names appear in the reviewed list as client tools to Claude.
Have a backend MCP client connect to the vendor, expose reviewed read and update tools with fixed definitions, and execute update calls only after approval by the responsible lawyer in the app.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's retention documentation marks the MCP connector (`mcp_servers`) as ineligible for ZDR: tool definitions and execution results follow standard retention. Ineligible features are not blocked for ZDR organizations; their data follows the feature-specific retention policy. In contrast, the Messages API and application-executed client tool flow are ZDR-eligible. MCP connector documentation states that servers can change tools at any time; client-side helpers for self-managed MCP connections convert MCP tools into Claude API tools. The decisive evidence is [ZDR scope], [reviewed definitions only], [read-only], and [minimize operated components, lower priority]. The first three eliminate {{option:A}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:D}}; the fourth identifies the correct answer's tradeoff.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Allowlisting and pinning satisfy definition control and read-only operation with the least operational burden, but connector tool definitions/results follow standard retention, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Claude-side processing uses only ZDR-eligible features, and the app controls tool definitions at the vendor → app → Claude trust boundary. The tradeoff is operating an MCP client and re-reviewing/deploying each vendor change; new tools become usable at least three business days later. This cost is acceptable because operational simplicity is lower priority.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It satisfies ZDR and read-only operation and follows vendor changes without deployment, but name-only filtering passes modified descriptions/schemas to Claude without review, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It satisfies ZDR and fixed definitions but exposes update tools, violating read-only operation and adding an approval-flow component.

Additional point: Remote MCP server documentation describes these as third-party services neither operated nor guaranteed by Anthropic, and recommends reviewing vendor security practices and terms before connection. Data sent to the vendor is separate from Anthropic's ZDR agreement.

questions.title: Balancing cost and retention in a ZDR contract-analysis service
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Legal's ZDR organization is building a client-contract PDF analysis feature. Conditions:

- Client contracts prohibit retaining original contracts at Anthropic outside the ZDR agreement.
- Lawyers ask around ten questions about the same roughly 150-page contract at 2–3 minute intervals. Latency and input cost from the second question onward are concerns.
- Clause extraction uses a JSON schema. Experiments show that client-specific schemas with the company name in `enum` improve accuracy, but client names are themselves confidential and must not remain in any form beyond request processing.
- Around 300 contracts are reviewed together each midnight, and results must be ready for the 8 a.m. meeting. Finance approves up to twice the estimate based on discounted batch pricing.

Which design is **most appropriate** under Anthropic documentation?

options.text: Use inline PDFs, omit `cache_control` because caches also remain in server memory, extract clauses with a shared schema, and run overnight review with ordinary Messages API calls.
Add `cache_control` to inline PDF document blocks, extract clauses with a shared schema, and submit the same cached blocks to Message Batches for both batch and cache discounts.
Add `cache_control` to inline PDF document blocks, extract clauses with a shared schema containing no client information, and parallelize ordinary Messages API calls for overnight review.
Add `cache_control` to inline PDF document blocks, improve accuracy with client-specific schemas containing company names in `enum`, and use ordinary Messages API calls overnight.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic retention documentation marks the Messages API, PDF support, and prompt caching as ZDR-eligible: KV cache representations and hashes remain only in memory during the cache TTL and are deleted after expiry. Structured outputs are "Yes (qualified)": the JSON schema alone is cached for up to 24 hours after last use. The same guidance warns against sensitive data in schema property names, `enum`/`const` values, or `pattern`. Message Batches retain data for 29 days for asynchronous processing and are not ZDR-eligible. Batch documentation offers a 50% discount and says most finish within an hour but expire if unfinished after 24 hours. PDF guidance recommends prompt caching for repeated questions. The decisive evidence is [ZDR scope], [latency/cost from the second question], [no client-name retention], and [8 a.m. deadline and double budget]: these eliminate {{option:B}}, {{option:A}}, and {{option:D}}, while the final constraint establishes affordability.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Caching is ZDR-eligible, so there is no reason to avoid it. Reprocessing 150 pages for every question leaves latency and cost concerns unresolved.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It is cheapest, but batch retention of 29 days violates the first condition. Completion is also not assured before the 24-hour window, risking the eight-hour deadline.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It delivers caching, schema output, and bulk processing using only ZDR-eligible features. The tradeoff is losing the batch discount, bringing overnight cost to twice the batch estimate—the approved ceiling—while managing concurrency/rate limits and forgoing client-specific schema accuracy gains.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It offers the highest accuracy, but schemas containing company names remain cached for up to 24 hours after last use, violating the third condition.

Additional point: Files API storage (until deletion/expiry) and code execution (containers up to 30 days) are also ineligible for ZDR. Even in ZDR organizations, flagged content and legally required retention are excluded from ZDR.

questions.title: Preserving trace observability without customer content
questions.prompt:
Nuri Fintech operates a support agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK. It has no ZDR agreement. Security requirements:

- **Keep viewing** agent flow, tool-call order, and latency in OpenAI's Traces dashboard.
- **Do not retain** original customer-support content, tool arguments, or tool results in OpenAI-side traces.
- Send **the same trace structure** to the internal SIEM for anomaly detection; original content is unnecessary.

According to Agents SDK documentation, choose **two settings to apply together**.

options.text: Set `RunConfig.trace_include_sensitive_data` to `False` to omit inputs and outputs from generation and function-call spans.
Register an internal SIEM processor using `set_trace_processors()`, sending traces to the internal backend and managing export routes through one processor list.
Add an internal SIEM processor using `add_trace_processor()` to send traces to the internal backend alongside default OpenAI export.
Disable tracing globally with `set_tracing_disabled(True)` and manually log agent flow and tool-call order in application logs sent to the SIEM.
Leave `trace_include_sensitive_data` at its default and add a SIEM processor with `add_trace_processor()` that sends only spans with input/output fields removed to the SIEM.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK tracing is enabled by default, and `generation_span()` and `function_span()` record LLM-generation and function-call inputs/outputs. Disabling `trace_include_sensitive_data` (default `True`) omits that content. Adding a custom processor with `add_trace_processor()` preserves default OpenAI export; `set_trace_processors()` replaces default processors. Key clues are [keep the dashboard], [no original content at OpenAI], and [same structure in the SIEM]. Only {{option:A}} plus {{option:C}} meets all three.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Retains span structure while omitting original input/output content.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Replaces the default processor, cutting off traces to OpenAI's dashboard.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Preserves default export and sends the same traces to the SIEM. With {{option:A}}, both receive structure without original content.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Disabling tracing prevents use of the Traces dashboard, and the SIEM receives custom logs rather than the SDK trace structure.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The SIEM does not receive original content, but the default setting still includes inputs/outputs in spans sent through default OpenAI export, violating the second condition.

Also note: The documentation says tracing is unavailable to organizations using OpenAI APIs under ZDR. If original content must go only to internal systems and successful masking must be a condition of export, the documentation recommends putting masking and forwarding in one custom exporter configured through `set_trace_processors()`.

questions.title: Reducing Google-side exposure while retaining Gemini debugging logs

A team runs an insurance-advice app with the Gemini API in a billing-enabled Cloud project. Requirements:

- **Minimize the amount and retention period** of prompts/responses retained by Google, and ensure data **is not used for product improvement**.
- Personal advice questions can be answered without web evidence, while general policy questions benefit from current web sources. Google Search grounding is currently enabled for every request.

According to Gemini API documentation, **which configuration is most appropriate**?

options.text: Disable project logging and troubleshoot incidents using Google's abuse-monitoring records. Disable search grounding for personal advice and enable it only for general policy questions.
Set log retention to seven days and do not share datasets, but keep search grounding enabled for every request because grounded answers are better.

Set log retention to seven days and join Contributor Tier for token discounts on some models to offset higher analysis costs. Disable grounding for personal advice and enable it only for general policy questions.
Set log retention to seven days, do not share datasets or join Contributor Tier, and disable search grounding for personal advice while enabling it only for general policy questions.

questions.explanation:
Project owners enable Gemini API logs in billing-enabled projects. Retention defaults to 55 days, with 7, 14, 28, or 55 days selectable in AI Studio. Billing-project logs are not used for product improvement by default, but sharing datasets or joining Contributor Tier subjects data to unpaid-service terms, allowing product improvement and model training/evaluation. The terms state that Google Search grounding stores prompts, context, and outputs for 30 days. Key clues are [one week of logs], [minimum amount/retention and no product improvement], and [grounding only when needed].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Abuse-monitoring retention serves policy-violation detection, not developer debugging, and is separate from project logs. It does not meet the one-week log requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Logging and data-use settings fit, but grounding retains even personal-advice prompts/responses for 30 days despite requiring no web evidence, violating minimization.

questions.title: Scope and tooling for an adversarial regression-testing program
questions.prompt:
Nuri Pay security is designing an adversarial testing program for an OpenAI-model payment-support agent, running from October 2026 through September 2027. Nuri Pay is an OpenAI enterprise customer. Conditions:

- The agent calls lookup/refund endpoints in a partner's payment SaaS. The contract has no security-testing clause; written consent has been requested, with a reply expected in January 2027. Internal policy forbids attack testing against unauthorized external assets.
- The draft uses graders on the OpenAI Evals platform for a regression set rerun whenever the model changes.
- The release committee compares "legitimate payment-inquiry success rate" and "attack success rate" when approving model changes.
- Misuse of refund tools through partner endpoints is the red team's top risk.

Which revision is **most appropriate**?

Combine legitimate-inquiry evaluation and adversarial cases in OpenAI Evals platform graders for every model change, adding partner endpoints to the same regression set after written consent.
Submit the agent to enterprise-managed OpenAI Red Teaming, including partner endpoints through integration test accounts, while continuing legitimate-inquiry evaluation in internal CI.

Include partner endpoints after written consent; meanwhile run Promptfoo adversarial sets in internal CI for each model change, reporting attack success rate alone because attacks are riskier than legitimate inquiries.

The decisive evidence is [program duration], [partner consent pending and internal policy], [the committee's two metrics], and [refund-tool misuse is the top risk]. - **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: An owned mock server respects authorization while testing the top-risk tool-misuse path immediately, and internal CI supports both metrics throughout the program. - **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Scope handling and metrics are correct, but the regression set depends on a platform becoming read-only one month into the program and shutting down after two months.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Enterprise customers can use the managed service, but third-party asset analysis requires OpenAI's written permission; absent partner consent also violates internal policy.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Scope and runtime are suitable, but omitting normal-behavior evaluation removes one required metric. The top-risk partner path also remains untested until January.

questions.title: Red-team priorities targeting residual risks in a Model Armor filter

- Users converse across multiple turns and send **error screenshots and description text together in one request**.
- The app server **decodes** Base64/URL-encoded strings in user input **before** calling Model Armor.
- Audio/video input is not accepted.

The red-team budget covers only two categories. Select the **two highest priorities** that **Model Armor alone does not cover and that this app actually exposes**.

Attempts staged incrementally over multiple turns
Very short imperative input of fewer than three words
Input mixing text and images in one request

questions.title: Dependency order of deliverables in prerelease adversarial testing
questions.prompt:
Nuri Health is conducting prerelease adversarial testing of a Gemini API medication-counseling chatbot using Google's generative-AI workflow. Conditions:

- Product safety policy includes service-specific rules such as prohibiting instructions to change individual dosages, beyond banning toxic language.
- Public benchmarks cover toxicity and stereotypes but scarcely cover service-specific rules.
- Synthetic tools expand supplied seeds: missing areas remain missing, while biases are amplified. Because synthesis costs money, use it only for gaps identified by seed analysis.
- Human raters can review only part of all outputs; the release committee decides using per-policy safety rates and failures.

Arrange these seven steps in the **correct dependency order**.

- (1) Generate outputs from the set, label them with a safety classifier, and have humans review and correct uncertain labels.
- (2) Expand queries synthetically only for gaps identified in seed analysis, completing the test set.
- (3) Map prohibited product-policy items to failure types and define use cases, edge cases, and lexical/semantic diversity targets.
- (4) Report per-policy safety rates and failures to release decision-makers and improve safeguards such as filters and blocklists.
- (5) Establish policy/use-case baselines with public benchmarks and identify uncovered or frequently failing failure types.
- (6) Manually write dozens of realistic seed queries for each selected failure type.
- (7) Analyze seed lexical/semantic diversity, policy/use-case coverage, and quality—duplication, adversarial character, and noise—and mark gaps.

items.text: Generate outputs from the set, label them with a safety classifier, and have humans review and correct uncertain labels.
Expand queries synthetically only for gaps identified in seed analysis, completing the test set.
Map prohibited product-policy items to failure types and define use cases, edge cases, and lexical/semantic diversity targets.
Report per-policy safety rates and failures to release decision-makers and improve safeguards such as filters and blocklists.
Establish policy/use-case baselines with public benchmarks and identify uncovered or frequently failing failure types.
Manually write dozens of realistic seed queries for each selected failure type.
Analyze seed lexical/semantic diversity, policy/use-case coverage, and quality—duplication, adversarial character, and noise—and mark gaps.

questions.explanation:
Google's workflow has four stages: identify testing inputs, find/create datasets, generate and annotate outputs, and report/mitigate. Dataset work first assesses existing coverage of policies and use cases to establish a baseline, creates small manual seed sets for gaps, expands them synthetically, and analyzes diversity, coverage, and quality. Safety classifiers assist labeling, but uncertain labels need human review because accuracy may be limited. Here dependencies determine the order, and the stated synthetic-tool conditions require seed analysis before expansion.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Define failure types, use cases, and diversity goals | Starting point; all policy items define test scope. | Identify inputs for testing |
| 2 | (5) Benchmark baseline and weak failure types | Coverage can be assessed only against the policies/use cases defined in (3). | Find datasets |
| 3 | (6) Write seeds manually | Gaps selected in (5), including service-specific rules, determine seed targets. | Create datasets |
| 4 | (7) Analyze seeds | Requires seeds from (6), using diversity goals from (3); identifies synthesis targets. | Analyze datasets |
| 5 | (2) Expand only gaps synthetically | Uses gaps marked in (7); expanding earlier amplifies seed omissions and bias. | Create datasets |
| 6 | (1) Generate, classify, and human-review uncertainty | Uses the completed set from (2); limited raters focus on uncertain labels. | Generate and annotate model outputs |
| 7 | (4) Report safety rates and mitigate | Labels from (1) supply metric calculations. | Report and mitigate |

questions.title: Separating refusal rates accurately after stronger defenses
questions.prompt:
A Claude API team is rebuilding its refusal dashboard after strengthening jailbreak defenses. Requirements:

- Aggregate **both** streaming responses and Message Batches results.
- Show refusals **by category** to identify policy areas, while **missing none**.
- On refusal, the client retries another Claude model. Distinguish **first-attempt refusals** caused by stronger defenses from **the final refusals users experience**.

Which aggregation method is **most accurate**?

options.text: For streaming, count refusals in `message_delta`; for batches, in succeeded results. Group by `stop_details.category`, put `null` in its own bucket, and separately record initial and post-fallback outcomes.
Count HTTP 4xx and batch errored results as refusals by policy area, remove cases where fallback succeeds, and show only the user-experienced refusal rate.

For streaming and batches, count only `stop_reason` of `"refusal"` with a populated `stop_details.category`, ensuring category totals equal the overall refusal count, and separate pre/post-fallback results.
Count `stop_reason` of `"refusal"` by category, immediately resend the same history to the same model, and classify only repeated refusals as final refusals distinct from the initial attempt.

questions.explanation:
For Claude 4 and later, streaming-classifier intervention returns HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`; streaming includes `stop_details` in the `message_delta` event. `stop_details` is always present on refusal, but `category` and `explanation` can be `null`. Refused Message Batches requests return as succeeded results. Documentation recommends retrying a different model instead of the same one, and modifying the triggering turn or resetting the conversation after refusal. The decisive evidence is [both streaming and batches], [categories without omissions], and [initial versus final outcomes].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It captures actual refusal signals in both paths, retains `null` categories, and separates fallback stages to isolate the effect of stronger defenses.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, confuses similar features)**: Streaming-classifier refusals are not HTTP errors or batch errored results. Removing initial refusals also violates the third requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: It omits refusals whose `category` is `null`.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, applies to a different situation)**: Resending the same history to the same model usually produces another refusal; documentation explains that refusals can continue without resetting context. This distorts final-outcome metrics.

Additional point: Ordinary text responses in which the model declines on its own do not have `stop_reason: "refusal"`. Over-refusal evaluation therefore separately requires reviewing response content for legitimate requests.

**References**: [Handle streaming refusals › API response format](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals) · [Handle streaming refusals › Best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals)

questions.title: The first action that balances containment and availability
questions.prompt: Considering [Incident] and [Requirements 1–3], **what should security do first**?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Onnuri Claims Adjustment is a midsize company handling insurance-claim consultations. It has five security staff and a legal team. All consultation services use the OpenAI API. OpenAI has approved the organization for Modified Abuse Monitoring (MAM), which is active.
>
> [Existing environment] The web-support agent calls the Responses API from the backend, leaves `store` unspecified, and continues conversations with `previous_response_id`. Customer-uploaded claim PDFs are uploaded to `/v1/files` as inputs, with automatic expiry after seven days set at upload. The agent has function tools `lookup_claim` (lookup) and `send_summary_email` (email), both executed by the backend. `send_summary_email` sends claim summaries when requested; during deadline week, hundreds of legitimate emails go to customers themselves daily. Registered customer email addresses are in a separate CRM, with no backend integration yet to retrieve them per conversation. The backend's own database stores customer-to-response-ID mappings and tool-execution records (arguments, results, and file IDs read in each conversation). Voice consultations use the Realtime API. Headquarters moved last quarter.
>
> [Incident] On Monday morning, monitoring found 12 instances of `send_summary_email` sending other customers' claim summaries to unusual external domains. All followed the reading of a particular customer-uploaded PDF, suggesting indirect injection through hidden instructions in that document.
>
> [Requirement 1 — Availability] It is claim-deadline week: lookup and consultation functions **must not stop**. Preserve legitimate summary emails where possible.
>
> [Requirement 2 — Containment] Stop further external sending **immediately**.
>
> [Requirement 3 — Evidence preservation] Legal must preserve original inputs, outputs, and documents from affected conversations for submission to regulators. Limit preservation **to affected conversations** to minimize additional copying of other customers' data.
>
> [Requirement 4 — Notification] Internal policy requires determining the affected customer count and scope and starting notification procedures **within 72 hours**.

options.text: Immediately revoke and reissue the production project API key to stop external sending, then resume lookup, consultations, and summary emails together after deploying the new key. Leave the PDF and affected conversation records untouched.

Immediately delete the PDF and related files from `/v1/files` to prevent rereading the instructions, and set `store` to `false` on subsequent requests. Continue lookup, consultations, and summary emails.

Develop and deploy a backend check restricting `send_summary_email` recipients to the conversation customer's registered CRM address. Leave lookup, consultations, legitimate emails, the PDF, and affected conversation records unchanged while deploying it.

Remove `send_summary_email` from the backend tool list and refuse to execute generated calls; route summary-email requests to a queue for staff review before sending. Preserve lookup, consultations, the PDF, and affected conversation records.

questions.explanation:
In OpenAI function calling, the model requests calls but the application executes them. Stopping execution of a specific tool in the backend immediately closes that route. Safety best practices recommend human review of outputs with significant real-world consequences. Key clues are "must not stop / where possible" in [Requirement 1], "immediately" in [Requirement 2], preserving originals/documents in [Requirement 3], and "no CRM integration yet" in [Existing environment]. Availability, immediacy, and evidence preservation create competing demands.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Revocation addresses exposed or misused keys. Here the requests used a legitimate key; stopping all calls violates [Requirement 1], and the same route reopens after restart.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Deleting the document destroys evidence required by [Requirement 3]. Changing `store` and deleting files do not stop the email path, so [Requirement 2] also fails.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Restricting recipients to the customer's own address is a fundamental fix that preserves legitimate emails. However, developing per-conversation CRM lookup violates the "immediately" requirement. It is a permanent mitigation to implement after the first action.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Immediately closes only the harmful route while preserving consultations, lookup, and evidence. Staff review delays legitimate summary emails during deadline week and adds staff workload.

Also note: The headquarters move in [Existing environment] is irrelevant distractor information.

**References**: [Function calling](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling) · [Safety best practices › Human in the loop (HITL)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices) · [Safety best practices › Revoke compromised API keys](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.prompt: **Which plan best satisfies** both [Requirement 3] and [Requirement 4]?

options.text: Retrieve responses and download PDFs only for the 12 conversations with email records; determine the affected customer count directly from those 12 and start notification within 72 hours. Check voice consultations through internal records.

Query existing tool-execution records in the internal database to identify all conversations that read the problematic PDF's file ID and establish the affected set; download only their responses and PDFs, prioritizing items nearest expiry. Check voice consultations through internal records.

To avoid omissions, bulk-download all customers' responses and uploaded files retained over the past 30 days to an access-controlled evidence store, identify affected customers there within 72 hours, and check voice consultations through internal records.

MAM excludes customer content from abuse-monitoring logs. Key clues are unspecified `store`, seven-day file expiry, Realtime usage, and internal file-ID records in [Existing environment]; "affected conversations only" in [Requirement 3]; and "determine scope within 72 hours" in [Requirement 4]. - **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preservation is narrow, but the 12 records show only conversations that actually sent emails. Conversations that read the same document and looked up other customers' claims without sending are missed, understating impact under [Requirement 4].

questions.title: Classifying paths into model context by who controls the content
questions.prompt:
A security architect is threat-modeling five internal AI services, classifying their input paths by **who can currently write or change the content entering model context**. All five run in an internal cluster, and all input data passes through internal storage. For each service, choose the **most appropriate input path** for the content identified as the classification target. One option is unused.

| Service (classification target) | Input path |
| --- | --- |
| 1. An HR policy bot answers questions employees type directly into an internal portal after SSO login (target: the question in the input box) | a. Definitions written by an external vendor that the vendor can still change at invocation time (tool supply-chain path) |
| 2. A support assistant drafts replies when employees paste complete emails from external customers into its input box (target: the pasted email body) | b. Text written by the authenticated requester whose request itself constitutes an instruction (direct-input path) |
| 3. A work agent retrieves tool names and descriptions on every invocation from a vendor-operated MCP server (target: tool names and descriptions) | c. Instructions reviewed, version-pinned, and deployed by operations (trusted-instruction path) |
| 4. A vision app extracts items from receipt photographs uploaded by applicants (target: text in the photograph) | d. Body data written by a third party without instruction authority (indirect-data path) |
| 5. A translation service deploys a vendor-written prompt template after platform-team review, pinned to a commit hash (target: the pinned, deployed template) | e. Text existing only visually that bypasses text filters (multimodal hidden-text path) |
| | f. Data read from storage on the internal network (internal-source path) |

options.text: Definitions written by an external vendor that the vendor can still change at invocation time (tool supply-chain path)
Text written by the authenticated requester whose request itself constitutes an instruction (direct-input path)
Instructions reviewed, version-pinned, and deployed by operations (trusted-instruction path)
Body data written by a third party without instruction authority (indirect-data path)
Text existing only visually that bypasses text filters (multimodal hidden-text path)
Data read from storage on the internal network (internal-source path)

items.text: An HR policy bot answers questions employees type directly into an internal portal after SSO login (target: the question in the input box)
A support assistant drafts replies when employees paste complete emails from external customers into its input box (target: the pasted email body)
A work agent retrieves tool names and descriptions on every invocation from a vendor-operated MCP server (target: tool names and descriptions)
A vision app extracts items from receipt photographs uploaded by applicants (target: text in the photograph)
A translation service deploys a vendor-written prompt template after platform-team review, pinned to a commit hash (target: the pinned, deployed template)

questions.explanation:
Google SAIF distinguishes direct user prompt injection from indirect injection through documents, emails, websites, plugin input, and text within images read by the model. Trust depends on whether the party currently able to write or modify content has authority to instruct the model. The decisive evidence is [who can currently write or change it] and [all input passes through internal clusters/storage]; the latter establishes that source network is not the distinguishing criterion. Rows 2 and 5 are traps where superficial clues—pasted by an employee versus created by a vendor—point in the opposite direction.

| Row | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1-{{option:b}} | The author is the authenticated requester, and that person's request is the instruction. This is direct input. |
| 2-{{option:d}} | Although an employee pasted it, the target is the email body, written by an external customer without instruction authority. Only the requester's instruction to draft a reply is direct input. |
| 3-{{option:a}} | The vendor writes tool names/descriptions and can change them at invocation time; they enter model input directly. This is the tool supply-chain path. |
| 4-{{option:e}} | Text in the photograph is hidden text the model can read without passing through text filters. SAIF identifies this as a distinct multimodal case. |
| 5-{{option:c}} | Although originally vendor-authored, the template has been reviewed and hash-pinned by the platform team. The vendor can no longer change it; operations controls the fixed instruction. This distinguishes it from row 3, where the vendor retains control. |
| {{option:f}} unused | A storage network does not identify the author. Data in internal storage still belongs to {{option:d}} if written by a third party. |
