questions.title: Execution location and deployment for a vendor skill package
questions.prompt:
A platform team plans to introduce a vendor's report-formatting agent skill package, containing SKILL.md and Python scripts, into internal Claude-based automation. The threat model classifies it as supply-chain input carrying instructions and executable code. Conditions:

- While the skill runs, **there must be no path for sending data to external networks**.
- **Deploy once at workspace scope** so everyone uses the same reviewed version.
- Use the package **only after security has read and approved both SKILL.md and the scripts**.

Which execution location and deployment approach is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Commit the approved package to `.claude/skills/` in developers' repository and run it locally in Claude Code so everyone checking out the repository uses the same version.
Upload the approved package through Skills API for the Claude API code-execution container, moving steps requiring external calls into application code outside the skill.
Have each teammate upload the approved package to claude.ai and allow code-execution network access only to selected domains through administrator settings.
Because the vendor is reputable and full review is costly, first upload and operate the package through Skills API, replacing prior approval with retrospective execution-log review.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic documents different network conditions by skill runtime. Claude API containers have no network access or runtime package installation; Claude Code runs on the user's machine with full network access; claude.ai depends on user/admin settings. Sharing scope also differs: API skills are workspace-scoped, whereas claude.ai skills are personal. The guidance treats skills like installed software: use trusted sources and audit the entire bundle for less-trusted skills. The decisive conditions are [no external transmission path], [workspace deployment], and [approval before use].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: A repository commit provides consistent deployment and prior approval, but Claude Code skills run with full network access, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: A networkless container structurally blocks exfiltration paths and distributes the same approved package across the workspace. The tradeoff is that the skill cannot call external APIs or install packages: external calls must move into app code, and scripts must use preinstalled packages.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: Custom claude.ai skills are uploaded individually and cannot be deployed organization-wide by administrators, violating the second condition. Allowing selected domains also leaves transmission paths open.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates a constraint)**: The runtime fits, but operating before approval violates the third condition. The documentation warns that even reputable skills may become risky if dependencies change when they fetch external URL content.

**References**: [Agent Skills overview › Security considerations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview) · [Agent Skills overview › Where Skills run](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview)

questions.title: Assessing threat-model notes against OpenAI safety best practices
questions.prompt:
A junior security specialist reads OpenAI safety best practices and writes four statements in an internal chatbot threat-model memo. Mark each **Yes if correct, No if incorrect** according to the documentation.

1. Limiting how much text users can enter can reduce prompt-injection risk.
2. Capping output tokens is presented as a way to reduce potential misuse.
3. Even in a service without login, a session ID can be sent as `safety_identifier` in place of a user identifier.
4. Values such as email addresses may be sent verbatim as `safety_identifier` without hashing.

items.text: Limiting how much text users can enter can reduce prompt-injection risk.
Capping output tokens is presented as a way to reduce potential misuse.
Even in a service without login, a session ID can be sent as `safety_identifier` in place of a user identifier.
Values such as email addresses may be sent verbatim as `safety_identifier` without hashing.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI safety best practices recommend layered controls rather than a single measure: moderation, adversarial testing, human review, prompt design, user identification, input/output limits, reporting channels, and safety identifiers. The relevant evidence is in the sections referenced by statements 1–4—input/output limits and safety identifiers. This question turns on comparing the effect of input limits and the form of identifier values with the documentation.

1. **Yes**: The documentation says limiting the amount of user-entered text can reduce prompt-injection risk.
2. **Yes**: The same section presents output-token caps as a way to reduce potential misuse.
3. **Yes**: The guidance recommends session IDs for unauthenticated users. Realtime API uses the `OpenAI-Safety-Identifier` header.
4. **No**: The guidance recommends hashing values such as email addresses. The claim that raw values can be sent is incorrect under this condition.

questions.title: Reducing conversation exfiltration through image tags injected by retrieved documents
questions.prompt:
A team operates six customer-support agents built with ADK. Its web app renders agent responses directly as Markdown and HTML, and agents answer using retrieved external knowledge documents. Red-team testing demonstrated that hidden instructions in retrieved external documents can cause responses to contain image tags; loading those images can send conversation contents from the browser to a third-party server. The requirements are:

- Even if injection succeeds, **the browser must not send conversation contents externally**; protection must not depend on the model following instructions.
- Apply **one common policy across all six agents**, without modifying each agent's code.
- Because exfiltration occurs **during rendering**, at least one control must directly target that path.

Select **two controls to adopt** within these constraints.

options.text: Add system instructions prohibiting Markdown images and HTML tags, provide several examples of correct response formatting, and list prohibited expressions.
Escape model output before the web app inserts it into the page, preventing tags from executing as elements or loading external images.
Implement argument-validation guards in every tool of all six agents, rejecting calls whose values fall outside the allowed range.
Rotate the agents' service-account keys and reduce permissions to minimize the data their tools can access.
Register a Model Armor plugin at the Runner level to inspect inputs and responses, adding a PII Redaction plugin if needed.

questions.explanation:
ADK safety guidance explains that HTML or JavaScript in model output may execute in a browser, and indirect injection may generate image tags that send session contents to third-party sites; output should therefore be escaped before rendering. It recommends Runner-level plugins for applying policies across multiple agents, including ADK's Model Armor and PII Redaction plugins. The decisive evidence is [no reliance on model compliance], [all six agents at once], and [directly target rendering]. These three constraints respectively eliminate {{option:A}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: This is a useful defense, but it relies on the model following instructions, violating the first requirement. If hidden instructions override this rule, the output is still passed through unchanged.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It closes the rendering exfiltration path regardless of model behavior, and one change to the web app covers all six agents. The tradeoff is that some images and formatting appear as plain text, so permitted formatting must be defined separately.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: In-tool guards are recommended by ADK, but implementing them separately in every tool violates the second requirement and does not address rendering.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Least privilege is good practice, but it does not target the rendering path where exfiltration occurs, violating the third requirement.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: This adds input and response inspection at the Runner without changing agent code. Inspection calls increase latency and cost; {{option:B}} remains the final defense for output that inspection fails to catch.

**References**: [ADK Safety and Security › Escaping model output in UIs](https://adk.dev/safety/) · [ADK Safety and Security › Callbacks and plugins](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Combining controls for a potentially compromised remote MCP server
questions.prompt:
The security team at fintech company NuriPay is threat-modeling a connection to an external SaaS contract-management server through the OpenAI Responses API remote MCP tool. An external vendor operates the server. Assume it may be compromised or malicious and can extract anything in model context. The connector is essential to the legal team's work, so canceling the connection is not an option. Constraints:

- Prevent customer identifiers and account numbers from reaching the server **by design**, rather than relying on vendor reputation or assessment results.
- **Do not rely** on the model following system instructions.
- Reviewers can handle **approximately 40 approval requests per day**, while tools are called thousands of times daily.
- Data sent to the server must be available for **retrospective audit review**.

Select **two controls to adopt**.

options.text: Remove customer identifiers and account numbers from model context, retaining only the fields needed for contract lookup with pseudonymous keys.
Allowlist only `server_label` values that passed vendor security assessment, then set `require_approval` to `never` for subsequent calls.
Set approvals to `never` and instruct the model in the system prompt to exclude customer identifiers and account numbers from server calls, leaving filtering to the model.
Set `require_approval` to `always` for every tool, requiring a reviewer to inspect every argument of every call before approving it.
Retain logs of `mcp_call` arguments, server responses, and approval requests, and periodically sample them to review data sent to the server.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI documentation says remote MCP servers must be trusted and warns that malicious servers may extract sensitive data from model context. By default, approval is requested before sharing data with a server; the documentation recommends carefully reviewing and, where appropriate, logging what is sent. An approval applies only to a single call. `mcp_approval_request` shows the tool name, arguments, and server label, while `mcp_call` records arguments sent by the model and output returned by the server. The decisive evidence is [prevent by design], [no reliance on model compliance], [40 approvals], and [retrospective review]. Together these eliminate {{option:B}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:D}} and require {{option:E}}.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It reduces the exfiltration target by making sensitive information unavailable even to a compromised server. The tradeoff is that queries requiring identifiers become impossible or need a separate step to resolve pseudonymous keys.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Reliance on assessment contradicts the compromise assumption, and disabling approvals removes another means of blocking outbound data.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes approval workload but relies on model compliance, violating the second requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Human review of every call maximizes exfiltration prevention, but a capacity of 40 daily reviews cannot support thousands of calls.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: It enables retrospective review of outbound data without increasing approval volume. However, data already sent cannot be recalled, and detection depends on sampling. It must therefore be combined with {{option:A}}.

**References**: [MCP and Connectors › Risks, approvals and data sent to servers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp) · [MCP and Connectors › Approval and tool call items](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Reducing hidden instructions that resurface through long-term memory
questions.prompt:
A personal-assistant agent writes facts read from web pages, emails, and shared documents into a long-term memory file and loads it at the start of the next session. A threat-model review identifies a path where hidden instructions in a web page are saved in memory and resurface in later sessions. Constraints:

- Memory is a core product feature, and facts from the web, email, and documents **must still be recorded**.
- Thousands of entries are written daily, so **individual human approval is infeasible**.
- **No additional model calls may be made at session startup** (the first-response latency budget is one second).

Select **two appropriate methods** for reducing this threat within these constraints.

options.text: Change the write path so a human reviewer must read and approve every memory write before storage, queueing entries until approval.
Store only facts stated directly by the user, excluding web pages and emails from memory and discarding content from other sources.
Store provenance with each entry, including URL, sender, and recording time, so externally sourced content can be identified later.
At every session startup, use a separate classification model to inspect each memory entry, filter suspected injections before loading, and move suspicious entries into quarantine.
Pass loaded memory as tool results, and state in the system prompt that it is untrusted data rather than instructions and that any instructions found should be reported to the user.

questions.explanation:
Google SAIF explains that tools, memory, and retrieved data can be poisoned and lead to Rogue Actions, including hidden rules in calendar invitations that resurface later. Anthropic recommends placing untrusted content only in `tool_result`, identifying its source, declaring in the system prompt that it is data rather than instructions, and asking the model to notify the user if it encounters instructions. The memory tool documentation states that the application executes all file operations, so implementing safeguards is the developer's responsibility. The decisive evidence is [retain recording], [no per-entry approval], and [no additional model calls at startup], which eliminate {{option:B}}, {{option:A}}, and {{option:D}}, respectively.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It prevents poisoning most directly, but humans cannot approve thousands of daily entries, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It reduces poisoning paths but abandons the core feature of recording facts from external content, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Per-entry provenance enables identification of external content at read time and tracing of anomalous entries. However, provenance fields alone do not prevent poisoning, and they increase storage-format complexity and size.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: A classification layer is itself recommended for tool results, but adding model calls at every session startup violates the third condition.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: It treats memory as untrusted data without additional calls. Residual risk remains because it relies on model judgment, so red-team tests should include memory entries containing hidden instructions.

**References**: [Google SAIF › Risks (Rogue Actions, Untrusted content sources)](https://saif.google/secure-ai-framework/risks) · [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Indirect prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Memory tool › Security considerations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool)

questions.title: Designing controls for an unattended overnight computer-use agent operating supplier portals
questions.prompt:
A logistics company's security architect is threat-modeling an agent that uses Claude's computer use tool to enter purchase orders into 12 supplier portals. The agent views screenshots and performs clicks and typing; portal screens may contain externally authored content. Constraints:

- It must run **overnight without a person present**, finishing before morning reconciliation.
- Every portal requires **login**.
- Confirming a purchase order creates a **financial obligation**.
- One or two supplier portals are added each quarter, and portal domains occasionally change.

Which **control configuration is most appropriate**?

options.text: Run with least privilege in a dedicated VM and restrict internet access to an allowlist of the 12 portal domains. Include credentials for a dedicated account limited to order entry in the instructions so the agent can log in; a person confirms orders in the morning.

Run with least privilege in a dedicated VM and restrict internet access to an allowlist of the 12 portal domains. A person logs in during the day, and the agent completes order confirmation overnight; record every screen and click for morning review.

Run with least privilege in a dedicated VM and restrict internet access to an allowlist of the 12 portal domains. A person logs into the VM's browser during the day, keeping passwords out of model input; the agent only enters orders, and a person confirms them in the morning.

Run with least privilege in a dedicated VM and have a person log in during the day. Leave internet access unrestricted to prevent domain changes from blocking work, rely on the tool's automatic classifier for suspected screen injections, and have a person confirm orders in the morning.

questions.explanation:
Claude's computer use documentation recommends a dedicated VM or container with least privilege, withholding sensitive data such as login credentials from the model, restricting internet access to an allowlist of domains, and requiring human confirmation for consequential decisions such as completing financial transactions. It also explains that a classifier scans tool results such as screenshots and, when injection is suspected, prompts the model to verify instruction provenance. However, this extra protection may not be ideal for unattended use, and the preventive measures remain important even with the classifier. The decisive evidence is [login for every portal], [order confirmation creates financial obligations], and [unattended overnight]. The first two determine what the model may receive and which step belongs to a person; the last postpones human intervention until morning.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It provides isolation, allowlisting, and human confirmation, but exposes portal credentials to the model in instructions. Limiting the account to order entry does not change the fact that sensitive data is being passed in a way the documentation advises against.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It most reliably finishes before morning reconciliation, but automatically creates financial obligations overnight without human confirmation. Recording provides retrospective review, not confirmation before commitment.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It withholds login credentials from the model, leaves confirmation to a person, and restricts internet access to allowed domains. The tradeoffs are that confirmation waits until morning, expired daytime login sessions may stop overnight work, and a person must update the allowlist whenever suppliers or domains change.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes domain-change maintenance but abandons the allowlist, expanding exposure to malicious content and relying on the classifier. Unattended overnight execution is precisely a use case where the documentation says that additional classifier protection may not be ideal.

**References**: [Computer use tool › Security considerations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool)

questions.title: Where to place controls for rendering model output in a dashboard
questions.prompt:
An internal analytics dashboard renders model output as Markdown to show tables, lists, internal-document links, and company-logo images. A threat-model review identifies the path where unvalidated model output enters the UI (SAIF's Insecure Model Output). Constraints for selecting the control location:

- **Formatting**, including tables and lists, **must be retained**.
- The **result must remain safe** even if the model violates instructions or is deceived.
- **No additional model calls per request** are allowed within latency and cost budgets.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: At the renderer, pass Markdown through a sanitizer that retains only allowed elements and restrict image and link URLs to an allowlist of internal domains.
Put rules against HTML tags and external images, along with examples of allowed formatting, in the system prompt so the model writes only safe Markdown.
Escape all model output and display it as plain text without interpreting Markdown; provide a separate downloadable file for users who need tables.
Before displaying output, use a separate classification model to identify dangerous links and tags, blocking responses classified as dangerous.

questions.explanation:
SAIF defines Insecure Model Output as output reaching downstream systems or users without validation, rewriting, or formatting, and identifies Output Validation and Sanitization as a control. ADK safety guidance likewise recommends escaping model-generated text before inserting it into a UI. The decisive evidence is [retain formatting], [safe even when the model is deceived], and [no additional model calls], which respectively eliminate {{option:C}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Deterministic code constrains rendered output independently of model behavior while retaining tables and lists and avoiding additional calls. The tradeoff is maintenance of allowed elements and domains; new formatting requires a sanitizer-policy update.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It helps by design but relies on model compliance, violating the second condition. If hidden instructions override the rules, output is still rendered unchanged.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is the safest simple approach, but losing table and list formatting violates the first condition.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It acts as an output-validation layer, but additional model calls on every request violate the third condition, and the classifier's decisions are also probabilistic.

**References**: [Google SAIF › Risks (Insecure Model Output)](https://saif.google/secure-ai-framework/risks) · [Google SAIF › Controls](https://saif.google/secure-ai-framework/controls) · [ADK Safety and Security › Escaping model output in UIs](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Designing allowed network domains for the Claude Code sandbox
questions.prompt:
A development organization is defining the domains that shell commands in the local Claude Code sandbox may access. Builds and tests need only two public package registries and one internal API. Security requirements:

- Broad domains such as `github.com` or cloud CDNs **must not be allowlisted merely to avoid installation failures, creating exfiltration paths**.
- The threat model requires blocking **bypasses such as domain fronting**, which disguise an unlisted destination using an allowlisted hostname.
- Developers **must not expand allowed domains through their own settings or prompt approvals**.
- To maintain development speed, security must process new-domain requests **within one business day**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Put only the three required domains in managed `allowedDomains`, prevent user additions with `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, and retain the built-in proxy's hostname-matching control.

Put the three required domains plus `github.com` and registry-CDN wildcards in managed settings, prevent user additions with `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, and install a custom TLS-inspection proxy and its CA in the sandbox.
Put only the three required domains in managed `allowedDomains`, prevent user additions with `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, and install a custom TLS-inspection proxy and its CA in the sandbox.
Put only the three required domains in `allowedDomains` and install a custom TLS-inspection proxy and its CA, but let developers approve unlisted domains at prompts or add them to their own settings.

questions.explanation:
The Claude Code sandbox's built-in proxy makes allow decisions using the hostname supplied by the client and does not inspect TLS by default. Documentation warns that broad domains such as `github.com` can provide exfiltration paths and techniques such as domain fronting can reach destinations outside the allowlist. Stronger assurance requires a custom proxy that terminates TLS and inspects traffic, with its CA installed. `allowManagedDomainsOnly` permits only domains from managed settings and blocks unlisted hosts without prompting. The decisive evidence is [no broad domains], [block domain-fronting bypasses], and [no developer expansion through settings or approvals], eliminating {{option:B}}, {{option:A}}, and {{option:D}}, respectively. The fourth condition, one-business-day processing, defines the operational cost of the correct answer.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It minimizes and locks domains with little operational overhead, but the built-in proxy checks only hostnames and cannot prevent the stated disguise-based bypass, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: TLS inspection resists bypasses, but `github.com` and CDN wildcards are precisely the broad domains the documentation warns about, violating the first condition. It minimizes installation failures.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Minimal domains, locked managed settings, and a TLS-inspection proxy satisfy all three security requirements. The cost is operating the proxy, distributing its CA, and waiting up to one business day for security to process new domains.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It minimizes domains and inspects TLS, but developer approvals or personal-settings additions violate the third condition. It avoids waiting for new domains.

**References**: [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Network isolation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing) · [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Limitations (Security limitations)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)

questions.title: Choosing the enforcement layer for tool-loop cost exhaustion
questions.prompt:
A data-analysis agent built with the OpenAI Agents SDK offers a free trial. One trial user repeatedly submits ambiguous requests that trigger loops with dozens of tool calls, consuming most of the daily budget alone. The team is adding cost exhaustion to its threat model and choosing where to enforce limits. Requirements:

- Enforce limits in code **without relying** on model compliance.
- One user's runaway usage **must not block other users**.
- Legitimate trial users **must be able to complete** analyses requiring several tool calls in one request.

Which approach is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Add a system-prompt rule limiting tools to five calls per request, guide the analysis step by step, and instruct the model to stop itself if it exceeds the limit.
In the application, set each run's `max_turns` high enough for normal analyses and reject new requests when a user's daily token or cost budget is exceeded.
Set a low maximum output-token count, reducing tokens per response as a substitute for a per-user cost cap.
Lower the OpenAI project's rate limit to constrain combined usage across all users and thereby cap costs.

questions.explanation:
The Agents SDK's `max_turns` limits agent-loop iterations (LLM calls) in a run. Exceeding it raises `MaxTurnsExceeded`, and `error_handlers` can return an alternative final output. OpenAI's rate-limit documentation explains that limits apply at organization and project levels, not per user, and recommends daily, weekly, or monthly per-user usage caps, with hard caps or manual review when exceeded. The decisive evidence is [code enforcement], [protect other users], and [complete normal analyses].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It attempts to reduce calls through instructions but relies on model compliance, violating the first condition. Compliance is not guaranteed when ambiguous requests trigger loops.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Code bounds both per-run calls and cumulative per-user budgets, satisfying all three conditions. It requires per-user usage accounting and limit design; overly low limits cause legitimate analyses to hit `MaxTurnsExceeded`.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Documentation lists output-token limits as a misuse control, but they do not reduce call counts or prevent loop-driven costs, and may also prevent normal analyses from completing.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: When a runaway user consumes a project-wide limit, all users receive 429 responses, violating the second condition.

**References**: [Agents SDK › Running agents (max\_turns)](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/) · [Rate limits › Per-user limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits) · [Safety best practices › Constrain user input and limit output tokens](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.title: Handling a screener call that ends in refusal
questions.prompt: A developer operating a chat service through the Claude API sends user input to a small-model screener (Claude Haiku 5.5) before the main conversation. The screener returns an `injection_suspected` Boolean through structured output. Some calls begin ending with `stop_reason: "refusal"` and no classification value. **How should these inputs be handled?**

options.text: Treat screener refusal as a risk signal, block the input through the same path as `injection_suspected: true`, and count refusals separately.
Treat the missing classification as insufficient proof of a violation and pass the input to the main conversation, logging refusal counts for later batch review.
Repeat the same screener call without a retry limit until a classification appears, then handle the input according to that value.
Treat refusal as a service failure, tell the user it is a temporary error, and retain the input for later reprocessing.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic explains that Haiku 5.5's safety classifier may refuse the screening request itself and says to treat `stop_reason: "refusal"` as a harmful classification. The same rule applies when screening tool results; refusal means there is no classification value to read. The decisive evidence is [ends in refusal without a classification value].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Blocking refusals prevents unclassified input from passing. Legitimate but sensitive inputs may also be blocked, so false-positive rates should be measured separately using benign questions.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Treating refusal as safe creates opportunities to bypass screening and contradicts the documented handling.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; a method for a different situation)**: Sending identical input to the same model usually produces another refusal. Retrying with another model is a way to address refusal in a different situation, not a method for obtaining a security classification.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; factual error)**: Refusal is a normal HTTP 200 response, not an error, so it is not a service outage. Retaining the input for reprocessing allows unclassified input to pass later.

**References**: [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Handling stop reasons › Handle streaming refusals](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals)

questions.title: Handling the UI and conversation history when a streaming response is refused
questions.prompt:
A developer is building a streaming chat UI with the Claude API. Reports show responses ending with `stop_reason: "refusal"` after some sentences have already streamed to the user. Requirements:

- Detect refusal **from the response itself**, rather than through error-code monitoring.
- **Show guidance to the user** even if the refusal-reason field is empty.
- **Allow the conversation to continue** without recurring refusals.

Which handling is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Define refusal as an HTTP 4xx response, show guidance through error handling, and send the user's next turn with the conversation history unchanged.
Display `stop_details.explanation` verbatim if present; if empty, treat the response as normal completion rather than refusal.
If `stop_reason` in `message_delta` is `refusal`, switch the UI to a refusal state, show application-provided guidance, and remove the refused turn from history.
Immediately resend the refused request to the same model to see whether it returns a normal response, leaving conversation history unchanged while waiting.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic documents refusals as successful HTTP 200 responses with `stop_reason: "refusal"`, which error-rate monitoring alone misses. During streaming, `stop_details` arrives alongside `stop_reason` in a `message_delta` event. Because `category` and `explanation` in `stop_details` can be null, applications should branch on `stop_reason` or `stop_details.type` and provide their own guidance. Continuing without resetting history or removing the turn that caused refusal leads to repeated refusals. The decisive evidence is [response-level signal], [guidance even with an empty reason], and [continue the conversation], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Refusals do not arrive as error codes, so checking 4xx misses them; preserving the history also leads to repeated refusals.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It works when text is present, but documentation says `explanation` can be null and still requires refusal handling with application-provided text. It violates the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It detects the response signal, displays application-provided text, and cleans history so conversation can continue. Already streamed partial output cannot be recalled; the developer must decide whether to retain or discard it in the UI.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Resending the same context to the same model usually causes another refusal, violating the third condition. A retry should use a different Claude model.

**References**: [Handling stop reasons › Handle streaming refusals](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals)

questions.title: Result handling for refused requests in batch classification
questions.prompt:
A pipeline uses the Claude API's Message Batches to classify 50,000 documents daily. Its current result handler stores every `succeeded` result as a normal label. Some requests were refused without the team noticing. Requirements for the fix:

- **Refusals must not enter the classification-label table as labels**.
- A fixed monthly budget means **no wasteful repetition of identical input to the same model**.
- Daily results have a **same-day deadline**, so successful records cannot be reprocessed.

Select **two correct actions**.

options.text: Inspect `stop_reason` in every `succeeded` result and store `refusal` records separately from normal classification results.
Queue only `errored` results for retry, store all `succeeded` results as labels, and fill empty labels with a default value.
Resubmit refused records with the same input and model in subsequent batches until they pass.
Collect refused records separately and route them to human review or retry with a different Claude model.
If any refusal is found, discard the entire batch, revise the prompt, and resubmit all 50,000 records from scratch.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic documents refused Message Batches requests as `succeeded` results with `stop_reason: "refusal"`, not `errored`, requiring an explicit check. Resubmitting to the same model usually results in another refusal, so the recommendation is to retry with a different Claude model. The decisive evidence is [no refusals mixed into labels], [no repeated identical submissions], and [no reprocessing successes], respectively eliminating {{option:B}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:E}}.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Per-result refusal detection prevents contamination of the label table. It adds branching to result-handling code and requires separately tracking the refusal rate.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Because refusals arrive as `succeeded`, retrying only `errored` results causes refusals to be stored under default labels, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Repeatedly submitting identical input to the same model usually repeats the refusal and merely incurs cost, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It isolates refused records for another path without touching successful records. Different-model retries may change cost and quality; human review has limited throughput.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It may address the cause, but reprocessing successes within the same-day deadline violates the third condition.

**References**: [Handling stop reasons › Handle streaming refusals (Batch API, Retry guidance)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/handle-streaming-refusals)

questions.title: Migrating away from prefilling while removing secrets from prompts
questions.prompt:
A customer-support bot uses assistant prefilling with Claude 4.5 to maintain its persona. It also puts internal URLs and API keys in the system prompt and tells the model never to reveal them. The team is migrating to version 4.6 or later and redesigning prompt-leak protection. Requirements:

- It **must migrate** to the new model generation and cannot remain pinned to the old model.
- Preserve **consistent persona and tone**.
- Use a design where **prompt leakage causes no damage**.
- Avoid **reduced answer quality from prompt complexity**.

Select **two correct design choices**.

options.text: Stay pinned to the 4.5 model that still supports prefilling and retain the current never-reveal rule for leak protection.
Replace prefilling by separating persona and core instructions into the system prompt and reiterating them in user turns.
Replace prefilling with regex output post-processing to enforce tone, while leaving URLs and keys in the prompt and strengthening the prohibition rule.
Add more than 20 scenario-specific prohibitions and refusal examples to the system prompt to replace prefilling.
Remove internal URLs and keys that the model does not need from the prompt; perform required calls in server-side code and pass only their results to the model.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's prompt-leak guidance recommends separating core information from queries using the system prompt and reiterating key instructions in user turns. It states that prefilling is unsupported from Claude 4.6 onward. It also advises excluding information unnecessary to the task and using leak-prevention techniques only when needed because added complexity may degrade performance. The decisive evidence is [model-generation migration], [no damage even if leaked], and [avoid quality degradation], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It retains prefilling but violates the first condition against staying on the old model. Reliance solely on a prohibition also remains.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Separating and reiterating instructions maintains the persona without prefilling. It does not constrain the opening sentence as strongly as a prefill, so persona consistency should be checked with an evaluation set.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Post-processing can enforce tone, but keys remain in the prompt and leakage remains harmful, violating the third condition.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Although workable, adding many rules increases complexity and may reduce quality as the documentation warns, violating the fourth condition. It also fails to remove keys from the prompt.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: With no secrets in the prompt, leakage yields nothing sensitive. The tradeoff is implementing and maintaining server-side call code.

**References**: [Reduce prompt leak › Strategies to reduce prompt leak](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak) · [Reduce prompt leak › Before you try to reduce prompt leak](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-prompt-leak)

questions.title: Redesigning a chat app slowed by a preceding moderation call
questions.prompt: A team operating a chat app through the OpenAI Responses API calls the separate Moderation API before each generation request, increasing latency. Moderation scores **must still be retained** for audit records, and responses exceeding the threshold **must not be shown to users**. **How should the design change?**

options.text: Stop recording scores and make only the generation call, checking conversations with moderation afterward only if reported.
Cache preceding-call results by input-string hash, skipping moderation only for identical repeated inputs while keeping the preceding call for new inputs.
Send all responses first, then run moderation in a daily batch to find and delete over-threshold conversations retrospectively.
Request scores through the generation request's `moderation` parameter, then have the application hide over-threshold responses and record the scores.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's safety best practices explain that moderation scores can be requested alongside generation. The moderation guide says a top-level `moderation` object returns results in `response.moderation.input` and `response.moderation.output`. Scores are signals for application policy, not automatic blocking decisions; the application determines thresholds and whether to reveal responses. The decisive evidence is [latency from the preceding call], [continue recording scores], and [withhold responses exceeding the threshold].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes latency but abandons score recording for every request and cannot ensure over-threshold responses remain hidden.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Latency improves only for repeated identical inputs; the preceding call remains for most new inputs, leaving the root cause unresolved.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It records scores but checks only after displaying responses, violating the withholding requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It removes the preceding call and records scores from the same generation call. Because scores arrive after generation, violating inputs still incur generation costs, and the application must determine whether to reveal the response.

**References**: [Safety best practices › Content moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices) · [Moderation › Inline moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation)

questions.title: Covering the tool-definition surface excluded from inline moderation
questions.prompt:
A work agent based on the OpenAI Responses API uses function tools and third-party MCP tools with inline `moderation` enabled. A threat-model review identifies surfaces this inspection does not cover, and the team is selecting a compensating control. Requirements:

- Tool names, descriptions, and schemas are also model input, so **that surface needs controls**.
- **No additional inspection calls per request** are allowed within the latency budget.
- Third-party MCP tools **are required for the work and cannot be replaced with in-house implementations**.

Which compensating control is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Lower the inline `moderation` score threshold for tool-call arguments so tool-related input is blocked more readily.
Review tool definitions (names, descriptions, schemas) before deployment and pin their hashes; incorporate third-party changes only after renewed approval.
Inspect all tool definitions with a separate Moderation API call on every request, sending the tool list to the model only after passing.
Replace every third-party MCP tool with an in-house function tool to eliminate externally changed definitions.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's moderation guide says inline `moderation` covers tool-call arguments and tool outputs appearing in conversation content, but not tool names, descriptions, schemas, or response-format schemas. The MCP documentation also warns that third-party servers must be trusted and explains that tool lists are not fetched again while an `mcp_list_tools` item remains in context. The decisive evidence is [control tool definitions], [no additional inspection calls], and [no replacement of third-party tools], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:C}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Changing argument-score thresholds does not expand inspection to definitions and therefore fails the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Separate definition review and change control cover the surface that inline inspection misses. Vendor changes require renewed review and deployment, delaying adoption of new tools.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Definitions can be submitted to moderation, but an extra call on every request violates the second condition. Its harmful-content categories also do not guarantee detection of tool-definition tampering.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It provides the strongest definition control but violates the third condition against replacing third-party tools.

**References**: [Moderation › Inline moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation) · [MCP and Connectors › Risks and approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Designing streaming UX when moderation scores arrive late
questions.prompt:
A team operates a counseling app using the OpenAI API and streams responses to users. Inline moderation scores arrive only after the entire output has been generated. There are two flows:

- In the high-risk self-harm and crisis-support flow, **not even one character of harmful output may be exposed**.
- In the low-risk general-inquiry flow, **the first token must not be delayed** (one-second time-to-first-token target).
- There is **no budget for additional classifier-model calls** beyond the scores.

Select **two correct design choices** within these constraints.

options.text: Stream high-risk responses immediately, check scores after completion, and retract over-threshold messages and replace them with prepared guidance.
Buffer all low-risk responses on the server, check scores, and send only passing responses to the screen.
Buffer high-risk responses on the server until scores can be checked, then release them or substitute prepared guidance if over threshold.
Stream low-risk responses immediately, check scores after completion, and retract over-threshold messages and take follow-up action.
Stream high-risk responses while sending accumulated text to a small classifier after each fixed-length segment, stopping the stream if classified as harmful.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's moderation guide explains that streaming scores are absent from partial-output deltas and arrive only after generation completes. It also says scores are signals for application policy. Scores cannot prevent content already displayed before they arrive, so the application must choose release timing according to each flow's risk. The decisive evidence is [no high-risk exposure], [low-risk first-token target], and [no budget for extra classifier calls], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:E}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It avoids high-risk latency, but because scores arrive only after completion, harmful content is exposed before retraction, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Checking the entire low-risk response is safe, but delays the first token until generation completes, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Buffering only the high-risk flow prevents exposure. Its first character is delayed until completion, reducing perceived responsiveness.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: The low-risk flow meets its latency target and acts on scores afterward. Over-threshold output may be briefly exposed, so retraction UX and follow-up procedures require separate design.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It obtains intermediate classifications but adds classifier calls, violating the third condition. New characters can also appear between checks, so it cannot guarantee the first condition for high-risk flows.

**References**: [Moderation › Streaming behavior](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation) · [Safety best practices › Content moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.title: Designing Model Armor templates and floor settings for three business units
questions.prompt:
Three business units—security research, customer support, and HR—are building Gemini chatbots with Google Cloud Model Armor. Business-unit templates may be stricter than floor settings. Requirements:

- Security research handles legitimate queries such as malware analysis, so **legitimate queries must not be excessively blocked**. High-false-positive settings are unsuitable for this unit.
- The HR chatbot connects to personnel-record tools, so internal policy requires injection and jailbreak detection at **the most sensitive level, Low and above**. HR accepts increased false positives.
- There must be an organization-wide **minimum standard** that units cannot weaken.
- During the first month, **do not disrupt legitimate work** before examining blocking rates in logs.
- At most **one person per unit** is available for tuning.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Set the floor to Low and above, applying HR policy organization-wide. Use one template for all units, starting in Inspect only and switching to blocking after reviewing logs.
Set the floor to Medium and above, with every unit using the same Medium and above template in Inspect only, switching to blocking after reviewing logs.
Set the floor to Medium and above and raise only HR's template to Low and above. Start every unit in Inspect only, then switch units individually to blocking after reviewing logs.

Use no floor settings; let units manage their own templates, with HR at Low and above and the others at Medium and above. Start all in Inspect only and retrospectively audit changes through Cloud Logging.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor documentation explains that floor settings define minimum requirements for project-level templates within a resource hierarchy. Low and above detects subtle signals and carries a high false-positive risk, so it should be used carefully; Medium and above suits standard enterprise applications. Best practice is to start with Inspect only, examine blocking rates in logs, and then switch to Inspect and block. The decisive evidence is [avoid false positives on security research], [HR requires Low and above], [organization-wide minimum], and [no disruption in the first month]. The first three respectively eliminate {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It meets HR policy, but a Low and above floor prevents security research from choosing a less strict setting, violating its false-positive requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It provides a minimum, nonblocking first month, and low tuning overhead, but HR does not reach the required most-sensitive level, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: A medium floor establishes the minimum, HR alone is stricter, and units move to blocking after reviewing logs. The tradeoffs are accepting HR false positives, allowing violating inputs through initially without blocking, and assigning log review and adjustment to each unit's single owner.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Unit-specific levels and staged rollout are appropriate, but without a floor units can weaken settings, with only retrospective review, violating the third condition.

**References**: [Model Armor overview › Templates, floor settings, confidence levels](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview) · [Model Armor overview › Enforcement: inspect only vs inspect and block](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview)

questions.title: Operating Model Armor for unsupported languages and short inputs
questions.prompt:
A counseling app with many Vietnamese- and Thai-speaking users plans to use Gemini and Model Armor for prompt-injection and jailbreak detection. Short greetings and one-word replies are common. Requirements:

- Vietnamese- and Thai-speaking users **are part of the service audience and cannot be excluded**.
- Even where detection is not assured, **high-risk actions such as write tools and external transmission must be protected**.
- **No additional calls such as translation-model calls per request** are allowed.

According to Model Armor documentation, which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Detect languages absent from the supported list and reject those requests, changing policy to serve only users of supported languages.
Assume equal detection quality across all languages, trust only Model Armor results, treat `NO_MATCH_FOUND` on short input as safe, and operate without additional layers.
First translate every input into English with a model call, then inspect the translation with Model Armor so detection occurs only in a supported language.

Enable multilingual detection, do not interpret `NO_MATCH_FOUND` for unsupported languages or inputs shorter than three words as proof of safety, and disable write and external-transmission tools for those sessions.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor documents testing of responsible-AI and injection/jailbreak filters in Chinese, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. They may work in other languages, but quality may vary. Multilingual detection can be enabled per request or at template level. Injection/jailbreak detection returns `NO_MATCH_FOUND` for inputs shorter than three words because they contain insufficient information. The decisive evidence is [cannot exclude target users], [protect risky actions], and [no additional calls], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:C}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes detection uncertainty but excludes Vietnamese- and Thai-speaking users, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It provides no compensation for documented quality differences, violating the second condition, and mistakes `NO_MATCH_FOUND` on short input for safety.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Translation followed by inspection works, but the extra model call per request violates the third condition; translation may also alter attack wording.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It enables detection while incorporating limitations into the design and structurally restricting risky actions without extra calls. Sessions lose functionality, and restricted-mode criteria such as language detection and input length must be maintained.

**References**: [Model Armor overview › Supported languages](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview) · [Model Armor overview › Minimum word count and NO\_MATCH\_FOUND](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview)

questions.title: Configuring a Model Armor pipeline to remove PII before forwarding
questions.prompt:
A team is adding Google Cloud Model Armor to a counseling pipeline containing Korean users' names, card numbers, and contact details. Requirements:

- Remove PII such as card numbers **without blocking the entire request**, allowing conversation to continue.
- Handle **both** values pasted directly by users and values in model responses.
- **No custom masking service can be developed**.
- Log inspection history, but **do not retain raw sensitive information in logs for long periods**.

Select **two correct configuration choices**.

options.text: Develop a custom regex card-number masking service before Model Armor, sending only its processed text to Model Armor.
Enable Inspect and block with basic Sensitive Data Protection, blocking entire requests and responses when PII such as card numbers is detected.
Apply advanced Sensitive Data Protection only to the response template to remove values in model output, leaving the prompt template in basic configuration.
Apply advanced Sensitive Data Protection to both prompt and response templates, specifying infoTypes and de-identification transformations in SDP templates.
Because Model Armor inspection events in Cloud Logging can include snippets, review log retention and access permissions.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor documentation says basic Sensitive Data Protection supports inspection only, not de-identification, and handles a limited set of infoTypes such as credit-card numbers, primarily tailored to the United States. Advanced configuration uses SDP templates for detailed detection rules and supports de-identification such as transformation, tokenization, and masking. Input templates address uploaded sensitive data; output templates address sensitive-data leakage. Model Armor does not store content unless platform logging is enabled, but log events may include content snippets depending on configuration, and retention follows Cloud Logging settings. The decisive evidence is [remove without blocking], [both input and output], [no custom development], and [no long-term raw data in logs].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is a workable workaround but violates the prohibition on developing a new service.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Basic configuration cannot de-identify and only blocks on detection, violating the requirement not to block entire requests.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Responses are de-identified, but pasted user values receive only basic inspection, violating the requirement to cover both input and output.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Advanced detection and de-identification in both templates allow conversation to continue. SDP infoTypes and transformations require design and validation, and tests must verify rules against Korean user data.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Inspection history is logged, but raw data may persist in snippets, so retention and access must be controlled in Cloud Logging. Retention periods must balance audit requirements against personal-data minimization.

**References**: [Model Armor overview › Sensitive Data Protection: basic vs advanced](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview) · [Model Armor overview › Logging](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview)

questions.title: Can Agent Gateway's Model Armor alone protect MCP input?
questions.prompt:
An ADK agent deployed on Agent Runtime obtains tools through `tools/list` and reads resources through `resources/read` from a vendor's MCP server. The team plans to use Model Armor on Agent Gateway as its only prompt-injection defense. Constraints:

- Resource reading **cannot be removed from the workflow**.
- The external vendor's MCP server content **cannot be trusted**.
- The latency budget allows **only one additional inspection stage per request**.
- Limited agent-maintenance staffing requires **as few callbacks and plugins as possible**.

According to Agent Gateway and Model Armor documentation, which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Enable Model Armor on Agent Gateway and register one Model Armor plugin in the ADK agent to inspect MCP resource bodies and tool descriptions before they become model input.
Enable Model Armor on Agent Gateway with no additional controls, assuming the gateway inspects all MCP traffic.
Disable Model Armor on Agent Gateway, connect only to MCP vendors that pass security assessment, and trust server content based on that assessment.
Enable Model Armor on Agent Gateway, prohibit MCP resource reading, use the external server only through `tools/call`, and have people approve and incorporate required resources.

questions.explanation:
Model Armor's Agent Gateway integration documentation says MCP `tools/call` and `prompts/get` requests and responses, plus tool execution errors, are inspected. `tools/list`, `resources/*`, `notifications/*`, and MCP streaming HTTP/SSE are not inspected. Ingress inspection covers only ADK agents' `streamQuery`; document and file uploads such as PDFs are unsupported. ADK safety guidance says the Model Armor plugin inspects content at designated execution points. The decisive evidence is [resource reading cannot be removed], [untrusted server content], [one extra inspection stage], and [minimal callbacks/plugins].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: One agent-side plugin covers `resources/*` and `tools/list` content missed by the gateway. It adds plugin maintenance and one inspection call's latency; tests must verify that its execution points cover every relevant MCP surface.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: `tools/list` and `resources/*`, explicitly excluded by the documentation, pass through unchanged, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Trust based on vendor assessment violates the untrusted-content assumption and also abandons gateway coverage of `tools/call`.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It stays within gateway coverage but violates the first condition that resource reading cannot be removed.

Additional point: Gateway support is limited; payloads from agents using frameworks other than ADK are not inspected. First verify that the chosen framework is supported.

**References**: [Integrate Model Armor with Agent Gateway › MCP Coverage, Ingress, Limitations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/model-armor-agent-gateway-integration) · [Agent Gateway overview › Supported policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview) · [ADK Safety and Security › Callbacks and plugins](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Reducing Gemini safety-filter false positives in a medical-information app
questions.prompt:
A medical-information app sets every adjustable category to `block_low_and_above` in Gemini API calls. Legitimate patient questions about medication dosages or overdose symptoms are frequently blocked by `dangerous_content`. The team wants to relax filtering. Constraints:

- False positives are a problem **only in `dangerous_content`**; keep other categories at their current levels.
- Preserve the **`jailbreak` category** for prompt-jailbreak attempts.
- Since filters use probability, separately check for **low-probability but severe output** slipping through.
- The team must understand **Terms of Service responsibilities and possible review** for less restrictive settings.

Which action is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Relax only `dangerous_content`, retain `jailbreak` and other categories, add tests and application checks for low-probability severe cases, and verify possible Terms of Service review.
Set all adjustable categories to `off` to eliminate false positives at once, with no application checks or separate tests for content missed by filtering.
Keep filter settings unchanged, maintain a list of falsely blocked questions with reviewed canned answers, continue blocking unlisted questions, and update the list monthly.
Relax only `dangerous_content` and retain `jailbreak`, assuming probability-based Gemini filtering will catch severe content without separate tests or application checks.

questions.explanation:
Gemini API safety-setting documentation says categories without specified thresholds are off by default in Gemini 2.5 and later, and adjustable categories include `dangerous_content` and `jailbreak`. Core harms such as child-safety violations are always blocked and cannot be adjusted. Filters block by probability of harm rather than severity, so severe content can have low probability; testing is recommended. Less restrictive settings may be reviewed, and compliance with the Terms of Service is the developer's responsibility. The decisive evidence is [only `dangerous_content` is problematic], [retain `jailbreak`], [low-probability severe output], and [Terms of Service responsibilities and review].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: It adjusts only the problematic category, retains jailbreak defense, addresses probability-based blind spots with tests and application checks, and clarifies responsibilities in advance. Creating and maintaining tests and checks costs resources, and some false positives may remain.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes false positives but also relaxes other categories and `jailbreak`, violating the second condition, with no application checks.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Leaving filters unchanged does not increase risk, but varied patient questions cannot be covered by canned answers, so it fails to resolve the false-positive problem in the first condition.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Category adjustment is appropriate, but ignoring that filtering uses probability rather than severity violates the third condition.

**References**: [Safety settings › Adjustable categories and thresholds](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/safety-settings) · [Safety settings › Probability vs. severity](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/safety-settings) · [Safety settings › Terms of Service review](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/safety-settings)

questions.title: Graduated responses to jailbreak attempts by authenticated analysts
questions.prompt:
A bank's fraud-response team operates an internal fraud-analysis assistant using an LLM API. About 200 analysts authenticate with SSO. The assistant explains fraud techniques and interprets detection signals in suspicious transactions. Security wants to address the risk of one analyst repeatedly trying policy-bypass prompts across different sessions. Requirements:

- Legitimate questions often contain terms such as forgery, identity theft, and limit circumvention. **Minimize false positives** to avoid delaying case handling.
- Additional latency per request permits **only one lightweight-model call**.
- Track repeated attempts cumulatively **per employee, not per session**.
- **Do not suspend an account after a single suspicious classification**, which would interrupt an analyst handling cases.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Screen requests with a lightweight model using the broad criterion 'Does this mention harmful or illegal activity?' Block flagged requests and automatically suspend an employee after three flags until security restores access.

Screen requests with a lightweight model using the narrower criterion of requests outside fraud-analysis duties. Block flagged requests and progressively add guidance, a requirement to explain the request, and administrator notification as the employee's cumulative count increases.
Block requests using a dangerous-word dictionary without a model call, automatically suspending an analyst after three flags in one session until security restores access.

Screen requests with a lightweight model using the broad criterion 'Does this mention harmful or illegal activity?' Block flagged requests and progressively add guidance, a requirement to explain the request, and administrator notification as flags accumulate within one session.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic describes screening input for jailbreaks and direct injection, where the user may be an attacker, with a lightweight model (Claude Haiku 5.5) and structured output. It recommends considering adjusted responses, restrictions, or blocking for users who repeatedly trigger refusals, and continually analyzing output to refine defenses. The classification prompt defines screening criteria, so the service determines what constitutes a violation. Documentation says to consider restrictions or blocking without prescribing escalation steps; graduated friction is a design judgment. OpenAI's safety best practices also recommend registration and login, enabling authenticated employee IDs as the aggregation key. The decisive evidence is [minimize false positives], [aggregate per employee], and [no account suspension]. Distractors violate different combinations of these constraints.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Employee-level tracking is appropriate, but broad criteria flag most legitimate requests to explain fraud techniques, violating the false-positive requirement. Automatic suspension after three flags interrupts analysts' work and violates the no-suspension condition.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Duty-specific criteria reduce false positives, screening remains one call, and employee-level cumulative tracking adds friction gradually while preserving account access. Attempts disguised as work questions may pass; per-employee state must be stored and operated; falsely flagged analysts still encounter friction such as explanation requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Avoiding model calls best meets latency constraints, but risky words occur frequently in legitimate questions, producing many false positives. Session-level counts reset when sessions change, and automatic suspension interrupts work.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Graduated friction is appropriate, but broad criteria produce false positives, and session-only counts reset in new sessions, violating employee-level aggregation.

Additional point: If screening ends in refusal without a classification, documentation says to treat it as a violation. Whether to add such cases to employee-level counts should be decided separately based on false-positive impact.

**References**: [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks) · [Safety best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/safety-best-practices)

questions.title: Prescreening harassment and hate in screenshots without captions
questions.prompt:
A customer-support app built with the OpenAI API prescreens uploaded screenshots before passing them to its support model. Most images have no captions, and harassment or hate may appear as text inside the image. Requirements:

- **Score harassment and hate in image text during prescreening**.
- Prescreening uses **at most two API calls per image** within the latency budget.
- **Do not send user images to third-party services outside OpenAI**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Send only the image to the Moderation endpoint (`omni-moderation-latest`) for scores in one call, forwarding low-scoring images to the support model.
Extract image text with an external OCR service, then send both extracted text and image to the Moderation endpoint for scoring in one call.

Use a vision-capable generation model to transcribe the text, send the text and image to Moderation, and, if results are ambiguous, show the image to the same generation model again for a final judgment.
Call a vision-capable generation model once to transcribe image text, then send the transcription and image together to the Moderation endpoint for scoring.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's moderation guide says `omni-moderation-latest` accepts text and images and the endpoint is free. However, categories including `harassment`, `hate`, `illicit`, and `sexual/minors` are text-only: image-only input receives scores of zero in these categories, and text must accompany the image for scoring. The decisive evidence is [score text inside images], [at most two calls], and [no third-party service]. The first requires supplying text alongside the image; the other two constrain how that text is obtained.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It uses one free call, but captionless images receive zero for text-only categories, so harassment and hate in their text are not scored.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Supplying text enables scoring, but user images go to an external third-party OCR service.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves scoring and the data boundary, but another generation call for ambiguous cases increases the total to three per image, violating the latency budget.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: Two calls extract text and submit it alongside the image entirely within OpenAI. Every image incurs generation-model cost and latency, and scoring is limited by transcription accuracy. Text missed during transcription cannot be caught by text-only categories.

**References**: [Moderation › Content classifications, Inline moderation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation)

questions.title: Choosing fail-open or fail-closed behavior by flow when screening fails
questions.prompt:
A payment provider sends user input first to a lightweight-model screener that returns a violation Boolean through structured output, forwarding only passing requests to the primary model. It already treats screener refusals without a classification as violations. The remaining issue is behavior when a timeout or server error prevents any classification. Two flows share the screener:

- Payment agent: invokes transfer and refund tools at users' request; executed transfers **cannot be reversed**.
- FAQ chat: a read-only flow answering from terms and fee documents, with Markdown links and images rendered in responses. It has a 99.9% monthly availability target, and **screener failure must not interrupt FAQ service**.
- **Ongoing costs from extra model calls on every request** have not been approved.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Pass requests in both flows when no classification arrives and mark their conversation histories for retrospective log review. Apply the same rule to payments, shortening review intervals from twice daily to every few hours and immediately notifying owners of anomalies.
Hold requests in both flows when no classification arrives and ask users to retry shortly. When the screener recovers, rescreen queued requests in arrival order.
Call a different second lightweight screener in parallel on every request in both flows, using the other screener's classification if one fails.

When no classification arrives, hold payment requests before tool invocation and advise retrying. Continue answering FAQs in read-only degraded mode with link and image rendering disabled, returning to normal when screening recovers.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic recommends lightweight-model screening and treating a refused screening call as a violation because no classification can be read. It does not prescribe behavior when timeouts or server errors prevent a classification; that decision depends on each flow's harm and availability requirements. The decisive evidence is [irreversible transfers], [99.9% FAQ availability], and [no ongoing extra cost], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:C}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves availability, but an unclassified payment request can immediately trigger an irreversible transfer; retrospective review cannot undo it, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It prevents side effects but also stops the read-only FAQ during screener outages, violating availability requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It provides resilience, but one additional model call on every request creates an unapproved ongoing cost.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It closes the high-impact flow while leaving the read-only flow open with reduced risk surfaces, specifically link and image rendering. Payments are delayed during outages, FAQ functionality is reduced, and unscreened input reaches the primary model in degraded mode.

Additional point: Both flows must retain the rule that refusals count as violations, independently of outage handling. Refusal is not merely an unavailable classification; it is already a signal to interpret as a violation.

**References**: [Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections › Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/mitigate-jailbreaks)

questions.title: Restricting an ADK agent's cloud API resource access to the organization
questions.prompt:
An internal reporting agent built with Gemini and ADK calls BigQuery and Cloud Storage through a service account. The security threat model includes indirect injection causing it to write data into a bucket in a project outside the organization. This quarter, the team wants to **deterministically restrict resources reachable through the agent's API calls to the organization**, without changing tool code.

According to ADK safety guidance, which control is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Rotate service-account keys quarterly and move them to a secrets-management service so leaked keys have limited lifetimes and accesses are logged.
Instruct the model not to write to resources in external projects and add an input filter for suspected injections to reduce attempts, logging flagged inputs.
