Place the agent's projects and APIs within a VPC Service Controls perimeter so API calls affect only resources inside that perimeter.
Escape model responses rather than rendering them directly in the browser, preventing external transmission through image tags or links in responses.

questions.explanation:
ADK safety guidance explains that running agents within a VPC Service Controls perimeter reduces exfiltration risk by limiting API effects to resources inside the perimeter. It also says identity and perimeter controls are coarse, so finer restrictions require tool-level guardrails. The decisive evidence is [deterministic restriction] and [no tool-code changes].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; confuses related capabilities)**: Credential management is good hygiene, but it does not restrict which resources a valid key can reach. Identity controls and perimeter controls are different layers.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Instructions and input filters are nondeterministic controls dependent on model judgment and detection accuracy, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: A service perimeter deterministically bounds calls without changing tool code. It is coarse and does not distinguish resources in other projects within the perimeter; perimeter policy must be designed and operated.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; addresses a different situation)**: It prevents rendering-path exfiltration but does not affect direct API writes by the agent.

Additional point: Tenant- or table-level restrictions inside the perimeter require in-tool guardrails comparing model-provided arguments with developer-defined policy.

**References**: [Safety and Security for AI Agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Two reinforcements extending .env protection beyond Read-deny rules into the sandbox
questions.prompt:
A platform security team deployed a managed `Read(./.env)` deny rule to Claude Code on developer PCs. Red-team testing identified two paths:

- Path 1: A repository script launched through Bash (`tools/dump_config.py`) can open `.env` itself and print its contents.
- Path 2: Claude can request an unsandboxed retry of a command that failed in the sandbox, then use that execution to modify project settings or hooks and weaken controls.

Constraints:

- Developers run tests and builds daily with `python` and `node` scripts, so **interpreter execution cannot be blocked**.
- Some internal tools are incompatible with the sandbox, so **developers must be able to approve unsandboxed retries**.
- The team already uses allow rules such as `Bash(python *)`.

Select **two controls that together close both paths**.

options.text: Add `Bash(python *)` and `Bash(node *)` to `permissions.deny` to eliminate scripts opening `.env`, and add `Edit(./.claude/**)` deny rules for settings and hooks.
Enable sandboxing and put the `.env` path in managed `sandbox.filesystem.denyRead`, blocking reads by all Bash child processes at the operating-system level.
Retain managed `Read(./.env)` and `Edit(./.claude/**)` deny rules while continuing to allow scripts without approval through `Bash(python *)` to preserve development workflows.
Add a managed `Bash(dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true)` ask rule, requiring developer approval for unsandboxed retries regardless of auto or bypassPermissions modes and existing allow rules.
Set managed `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` to ignore unsandboxed retry requests, requiring developers to run incompatible tools manually in a separate terminal.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code documentation says Read/Edit deny rules cover built-in file tools and recognized Bash file commands and redirections, but not arbitrary child processes such as Python or Node scripts that open files themselves; sandboxing is required to cover every process. The sandbox applies `denyRead` to Bash and its children, and by default protects writes to paths such as `.claude` settings, hooks, and `.mcp.json`, even against `allowWrite` or `Edit` allow rules. The remaining escape route is unsandboxed retry, which follows normal permissions: a matching allow rule such as `Bash(curl *)` can approve it without a prompt. An ask rule for `dangerouslyDisableSandbox:true` prompts even in auto and bypassPermissions modes and takes precedence over allow rules. The decisive evidence is [cannot block interpreters], [approved unsandboxed retries must remain possible], and [existing allow rules].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It closes path 1 but blocks interpreters, violating the first constraint.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: The OS boundary blocks access regardless of how scripts open files, and protected paths also block the sandboxed-write portion of path 2 by default. Incompatible tools may fail, and managed settings require deployment and maintenance.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Deny rules do not cover files opened directly by scripts, leaving path 1 open. Retries matching `Bash(python *)` are approved without prompting, so path 2 also remains open.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It preserves approved retries while closing the gap where allow rules suppress prompts. Every retry adds an approval prompt, creating developer fatigue, and approval judgment remains with the developer.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It closes path 2 but also removes approved unsandboxed execution for incompatible tools, violating the second constraint.

Additional point: Commands in `excludedCommands` run without filesystem or network restrictions, so using exclusions for compatibility takes them outside `denyRead` protection.

**References**: [Configure permissions › Read and Edit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions) · [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Protected paths](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing) · [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › The unsandboxed retry escape hatch](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)

questions.title: Replacing Bash argument patterns with structural controls for approved-domain access
questions.prompt:
A fintech platform team wants to restrict shell-command destinations for 400 Claude Code developers to internal staging servers and approved package registries. Developers must call staging APIs directly with `curl` to inspect headers and responses. Requirements:

- Requests **must not leave approved domains**, regardless of `curl` invocation form: option order, variables, absolute paths, or `sh -c`.
- Developers **must not expand domains through their own settings**.
- `curl` to approved domains must work **without approval prompts**.
- The three-person security team **will not operate a separate TLS-inspection proxy**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Enable sandboxing through managed settings, register approved domains as `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow rules, and enable `allowManagedDomainsOnly`. Sandboxed shell `curl` can reach only registered domains; other hosts are blocked without prompting.

Deny `Bash(curl *)` and `Bash(wget *)` in managed settings and permit approved domains only through `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow rules, leaving sandboxing disabled and other shell commands under normal permissions.
Enable sandboxing through managed settings but have developers specify approved domains in their own `allowedDomains`, approving unlisted hosts at prompts and adding them as needed.
Deploy a managed `Bash(curl https://staging.corp.example/*)` allow rule and block other `curl` calls with `Bash(curl *)` deny, reviewing rules quarterly.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code documentation warns that Bash rules match command text authored by Claude, so argument-restriction patterns can miss changes in option order, protocol, redirects, or variables; deny rules can also miss absolute-path invocations or calls inside `sh -c`. When network access must be blocked, use the sandbox network allowlist as well. `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow rules permit domains for WebFetch and also add them to the sandbox allowlist. With `allowManagedDomainsOnly`, only managed domains are recognized and all other hosts are blocked without prompting. The decisive evidence is [block regardless of invocation form], [developers cannot expand domains], and [no approval prompts].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: One list controls both WebFetch and shell commands, enforcing the boundary at OS level regardless of invocation form. New domains require managed-setting changes, potentially making the security team a bottleneck; tools using unlisted domains fail. The built-in proxy checks hostnames without TLS inspection, so broad domains can create bypass paths.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Deny rules plus WebFetch are a documented combination, but this team requires direct `curl`. Without sandboxing, absolute-path invocations and network access inside scripts are also not blocked.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Sandboxing is enabled, but developer-controlled allowlist expansion violates the second condition. Without managed locking, unlisted hosts can be approved at prompts.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Argument patterns are the fragile approach warned about in documentation, violating the first condition. Changing invocation form can evade denial.

Additional point: The sandbox wraps only shell commands. Built-in tools such as Read and WebFetch, hooks, and local MCP servers require separate permission rules.

questions.title: Preventing managed PreToolUse hooks from being disabled or bypassed
questions.prompt:
Security wants to enforce a PreToolUse hook (`check-command.js`) for 300 Claude Code developers, checking dangerous commands with an internal policy service. Requirements:

- Developers **must not disable this hook** through `disableAllHooks` in user, project, or local settings.
- Dangerous calls **must not pass** if the script crashes or the policy-service call times out.
- Developers **must retain their own formatter and notification hooks** in user and project settings.
- Decisions require internal policy-service logic over the full command body and **cannot be expressed using permission-rule syntax alone**.

Select **two correct configuration choices**.

options.text: Define the hook in managed settings. User, project, and local `disableAllHooks` cannot disable managed hooks, and developer hooks merge and run alongside them.

Enable managed `allowManagedHooksOnly`, preventing user, project, and local hooks from running and retaining only managed hooks. Have security review developer hooks and move them into managed settings.
Set `"onFailure": "block"` on the hook handler and exit with code 2 for blocking conditions. Startup failure, timeout, and unparseable output also block the action.
Replace the hook with all dangerous-command patterns in managed `permissions.deny`, eliminating hook-script failures.
Commit the hook definition to the repository's `.claude/settings.json` and require code review for changes so every developer receives the same hook.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code documentation says hooks configured through managed policy cannot be disabled by user, project, or local `disableAllHooks`; only the managed-level setting can disable them. Hooks merge across settings levels. Failed or timed-out hooks default to `onFailure: continue`, allowing the action to proceed, so policy hooks need `"onFailure": "block"`. Exit code 2 blocks tool calls in PreToolUse. The decisive evidence is [developers cannot disable it], [failure must not allow passage], [retain developer hooks], and [not expressible as permission rules].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Managed hooks ignore lower-level disabling while developer hooks still run, satisfying the relevant requirements. Security must distribute and maintain the script and policy service.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: This is the strongest managed-only lockdown, but also blocks developer hooks, violating the third condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It creates fail-closed behavior so dangerous calls cannot pass if the hook dies. Script failures or policy-service delays can also block legitimate commands and halt development.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It avoids hook failures, but permission-rule syntax cannot satisfy the fourth condition requiring full-command policy-service logic.
- **{{option:E}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: All developers receive the same hook, but repository hooks are not managed and are affected by `disableAllHooks`. Only managed hooks resist lower-level disabling, so the first condition is violated.

Additional point: `onFailure` requires Claude Code v2.1.295 or later and applies only to `command` and `http` hooks. The `if` field is a best-effort filter; enforced allow/deny decisions should be made in the hook body or permission system.

**References**: [Hooks reference › Disable or remove hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) · [Hooks reference › Block the action when a hook fails](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)

questions.title: Assessing the scope of Agents SDK tool guardrails and approvals
questions.prompt:
A team building a refund agent with the OpenAI Agents SDK has three requirements: (1) inspect every agent tool call with input guardrails; (2) execute refund function tools only after human approval; (3) retain conversation context while waiting for approval. Mark each design statement **Yes if correct or No if incorrect** according to the documentation.

1. Hosted MCP calls automatically use the same tool-guardrail pipeline as function tools, so requirement (1) is met without additional configuration.
2. Configuring input and output tool guardrails once on a local MCP server attaches them to all tools it exposes, satisfying requirement (1) for that server without per-tool configuration.
3. To block routing to an agent, attach tool-input guardrails to the handoff call; handoffs are inspected by the same tool guardrails as function tools.
4. Requiring approval for a refund function tool returns an interruption and resumable state instead of executing it; after approval, preserving context requires starting a new user turn and resubmitting the request from scratch.

items.text: Hosted MCP calls automatically use the same tool-guardrail pipeline as function tools, so requirement (1) is met without additional configuration.
Configuring input and output tool guardrails once on a local MCP server attaches them to all tools it exposes, satisfying requirement (1) for that server without per-tool configuration.
To block routing to an agent, attach tool-input guardrails to the handoff call; handoffs are inspected by the same tool guardrails as function tools.

Requiring approval for a refund function tool returns an interruption and resumable state instead of executing it; after approval, preserving context requires starting a new user turn and resubmitting the request from scratch.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK guardrail documentation says tool guardrails wrap `FunctionTool` and run on each call. Hosted tools and built-in execution tools do not use this pipeline, and handoff calls themselves are excluded. Local MCP servers can be configured with input and output tool guardrails, which the SDK attaches to every tool exposed by the server. Approval guidance says tools requiring approval return an interruption and resumable state instead of executing; resume the same run from that state. The decisive evidence is the scope addressed by each statement and which of requirements (1)–(3) it satisfies.

- **1 (No)**: Hosted tools and built-in execution tools bypass tool guardrails. Hosted MCP call controls belong to other layers such as approvals, so requirement (1) needs additional design.
- **2 (Yes)**: Server-level input and output guardrails attach to all tools exposed by that server.
- **3 (No)**: Tool guardrails do not apply to handoff calls themselves. Blocking routing decisions requires separately designing input-guardrail placement or other controls; function tools after handoff are inspected by tool guardrails.
- **4 (No)**: The first part, returning an interruption and state, is correct, but approval or rejection is followed by resuming from the same state. There is no need to restart through a new user turn, so its judgment about requirement (3) is wrong.

**References**: [Agents SDK › Guardrails](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/) · [Guardrails and approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/guardrails-approvals)

questions.title: Choosing where a coding-agent container should build images and push changes
questions.prompt:
A fintech platform team's custom coding agent runs in a fresh container for each task, containing only project source and temporary tokens. Outbound traffic passes through an egress proxy that checks requested hostnames without TLS inspection. Developers want agent changes to proceed automatically to container-image builds and pushes to the organization's GitHub repository. Requirements:

- Do not give the agent **privileges leading to host takeover**.
- Do not create **source-exfiltration paths to other repositories through broad domains such as `github.com`**.
- Builds and pushes must proceed **without manual developer work**.
- The two-person security team **cannot operate a TLS-inspection proxy and private CA**. These constraints take priority over iteration speed.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Mount the host's `docker.sock` into the container so the agent runs `docker build` directly. A CI stage outside the agent session receives a change bundle and pushes using its own credentials.
Add `github.com` to the agent container's allowlist for direct pushes. A CI stage outside the agent session receives a change bundle and builds the image.
Place a TLS-terminating proxy at the container's egress, allowing direct pushes only to organizational repository paths. A CI stage outside the agent session builds the image.
Allow container egress only to an internal package mirror and export changes as a commit bundle. CI stages outside the agent session build and push using their own credentials.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code sandbox documentation warns that allowing Unix sockets such as `docker.sock` effectively grants host-system access and can bypass sandboxing. It also explains that when a proxy checks client-supplied hostnames without inspecting TLS, broad domains such as `github.com` can provide exfiltration paths and domain fronting can reach outside the allowlist; stronger assurance requires a TLS-terminating inspection proxy. Although the documentation concerns Claude Code's sandbox, the same logic applies to socket mounts and hostname-based egress proxies. The decisive evidence is [no host-takeover privileges], [no broad-domain exfiltration path], and [cannot operate a TLS-inspection proxy], respectively eliminating {{option:A}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:C}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Moving pushes outside closes that exfiltration route, but the socket mount gives the agent host-reaching privileges, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It avoids host privileges, but opening `github.com` creates a path to send source to other repositories, and the proxy sees only hostnames, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is the documented stronger-assurance design and needs no manual work, but requires operating a TLS-terminating proxy and private CA, violating the fourth condition.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: The agent receives neither build/push privileges nor external routes; it exports only a change bundle for automatic continuation. A separate external pipeline must be built, iteration is slower because the agent cannot immediately see build/push results, and CI must validate the bundle.

Additional point: CI should treat agent-created changes as untrusted input again and apply static checks and review gates.

**References**: [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Security limitations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)

questions.title: Comparing socket access and command exclusions for docker compose in Claude Code
questions.prompt:
An integration-testing team of 80 uses `docker compose up` daily through Claude Code. Because `docker` is incompatible with sandboxing, security is comparing solutions. Requirements:

- No path may grant **host-level privileges without human approval**. A few approval prompts per day are acceptable.
- **Block** Claude from editing `docker-compose.yml` to add malicious service definitions and then executing them. This file may change only through PRs.
- **Build no new infrastructure this quarter**.
- Do not release other `docker` subcommands, such as image builds or `docker run`, **outside the sandbox**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Add `/var/run/docker.sock` to `sandbox.network.allowUnixSockets` so `docker compose` works in the sandbox, retain automatic approval to avoid prompts, and lock the compose file with an `Edit` deny rule.

Add only the required subcommand, such as `docker compose up *`, to `excludedCommands`, retaining normal permission approval prompts. Lock the compose file with both `Edit` deny and `sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite` so changes go through PRs.

Add `docker *` to `excludedCommands` to release image builds and execution together, retaining normal approval prompts. Lock the compose file with `Edit` deny and `sandbox.filesystem.denyWrite` so changes go through PRs.
Build a new isolated VM outside Claude Code sessions for Docker work and let sessions read only its result files, eliminating host access.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code documentation says `docker` is incompatible with sandboxing and recommends narrow `excludedCommands` patterns for required commands. Excluded commands run without filesystem or network restrictions but use normal permission approvals. Narrower patterns reduce unsandboxed scope. Tools such as `docker compose` derive behavior from working-directory files, so Claude could edit a compose file and then execute it outside the sandbox. Conversely, permitting `docker.sock` through `allowUnixSockets` effectively grants host access without approval because execution remains inside the sandbox. The decisive evidence is [no unapproved host privileges], [block compose-file tampering], [no new infrastructure], and [do not release other subcommands].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Avoiding prompts is convenient, but socket access grants host-level privileges without approval, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Only the required subcommand runs outside with approval, and locking both tool and subprocess write paths prevents tamper-then-execute attacks. Approval prompts remain, excluded commands lack sandbox protection, and every compose-file change requires a PR.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Approvals and file locks are present, but `docker *` also releases image builds and `docker run`, violating the fourth condition.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is the most conservative way to eliminate host access, but a new isolated VM violates the third condition.

Additional point: `docker compose up *` excludes only matching command text. Docker calls inside a `make` target or script, and absolute-path invocations such as `/usr/local/bin/docker`, do not match and remain sandboxed.

**References**: [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Run commands outside the sandbox with excludedCommands](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing) · [Configure the sandboxed Bash tool › Security limitations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing) · [Configure permissions › Read and Edit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)

questions.title: Amount-based refund approval with resumption hours later
questions.prompt:
A refund agent built with the OpenAI Agents SDK for Python uses `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`. Refunds are irreversible, and a run may refund several orders for one customer consecutively. Requirements:

- Refunds of KRW 100,000 or less must execute **immediately without waiting for approval**.
- Refunds above KRW 100,000 require a settlement officer's approval **for each individual refund**; one approval must not carry over.
- The officer responds **hours later**, and deployment may restart the web server meanwhile.
- Approval decisions **must resist forgery and replay**.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Pass an amount-over-KRW-100,000 predicate to `needs_approval`. Serialize interrupted run state into server-side storage; authenticate the officer, match decision IDs against interruptions, prevent replay, and resume. Store a version marker with the state.

Use the same predicate but keep the interrupted run only in the request-handling process's memory while waiting, resuming in that process. Ask customers to resubmit requests whose pending state disappears after a restart.

Use the same predicate, send serialized state to the officer's browser with the approval screen, and deserialize and resume the returned state with its decision unchanged. Require internal SSO and include a version marker.

Use the same predicate and server-side serialized state with officer authentication, decision-ID matching, and replay prevention. Approve the first refund with `always_approve=True` so later refunds in the same run do not prompt again, and store a version marker.

questions.explanation:
Agents SDK documentation says `needs_approval` accepts `True` or a predicate receiving call arguments. When approval is required, execution pauses and an item appears in `interruptions`. State can be serialized and resumed later; decisions are scoped to call IDs by default. `always_approve=True` applies the decision to subsequent calls of the same tool. The SDK does not authenticate serialized state, so keep it server-side, authenticate and authorize reviewers, match decision IDs against `state.get_interruptions()`, and prevent replay. Long-running approvals should store a version marker with serialized state. The decisive evidence is [approval per refund], [hours-long wait with deployment restarts], and [no forgery or replay].

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: The predicate lets small refunds proceed directly while high-value refunds pause individually in server-side state and resume after validation. State storage, reviewer authentication, replay prevention, and versioning must be implemented and operated. Refunds at or below KRW 100,000 proceed without human confirmation; calls whose arguments cannot be safely inspected bypass the predicate and require manual approval, potentially increasing reviewer workload.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves per-refund approval and immediate small refunds, but a deployment restart during the hours-long wait loses interrupted state and breaks the approval flow.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Resumption works, but entrusting unauthenticated serialized state to the browser and accepting it unchanged allows decisions and arguments to be altered. SSO does not guarantee state integrity.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Validation is present, but `always_approve=True` carries approval to later calls of the same tool, violating individual approval.

**References**: [OpenAI Agents SDK › Human-in-the-loop](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/human_in_the_loop/)

questions.title: Matching defenses when running claude -p in an untrusted repository
questions.prompt:
A team runs `claude -p` against external repositories in CI. The folder has never been trusted, and no trust dialog appears. For each situation, choose the **most appropriate defense** according to Claude Code documentation. One defense is unused.

| Situation | Defense |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Reject one server declared in the repository's `.mcp.json` for this run while continuing to use other servers in that file. | a. `--setting-sources user` |
| 2. Disable only hooks declared in project settings for this run while retaining other project settings. A disabling value in user settings is insufficient. | b. Add the server name to `disabledMcpjsonServers` |
| 3. Do not read repository settings files, including `.claude/settings.json`'s `env` block and helper commands, or `.mcp.json`, while preserving user settings. | c. `--settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'` |
| 4. Home-directory settings differ across CI machines, causing inconsistent results. Start without automatically loading hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, or `.mcp.json` servers from anywhere. | d. `--bare` |
| 5. Repository `permissions.allow` contains broad tool permissions, raising concern that these apply to `-p` in an untrusted folder. | e. No additional action; they are not used before trust |
| | f. `--permission-prompts none` |

options.text: `--setting-sources user`
Add the server name to `disabledMcpjsonServers`
`--settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'`
`--bare`
No additional action; they are not used before trust
`--permission-prompts none`

items.text: Reject one server declared in the repository's `.mcp.json` for this run while continuing to use other servers in that file.
Disable only hooks declared in project settings for this run while retaining other project settings. A disabling value in user settings is insufficient.
Do not read repository settings files, including `.claude/settings.json`'s `env` block and helper commands, or `.mcp.json`, while preserving user settings.
Home-directory settings differ across CI machines, causing inconsistent results. Start without automatically loading hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, or `.mcp.json` servers from anywhere.
Repository `permissions.allow` contains broad tool permissions, raising concern that these apply to `-p` in an untrusted folder.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code's 'What runs before you trust a folder' table says `claude -p` uses repository hooks, `env` blocks, and helper commands such as `apiKeyHelper`, and connects `.mcp.json` servers without prompting. Repository `permissions.allow` rules, however, are not used, and a warning is written to stderr. Documented defenses include `--setting-sources user`, `--bare`, passing `disableAllHooks` through `--settings`, and `disabledMcpjsonServers`. Each defense has a different scope, so the constraints determine the match.

| Row | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1-{{option:b}} | Only `disabledMcpjsonServers` rejects a server by name. It blocks that server across all session types without affecting others in the file. |
| 2-{{option:c}} | Project settings can override user-level `disableAllHooks` with `false`, so pass it through this run's `--settings`. Other project settings remain intact. |
| 3-{{option:a}} | `--setting-sources user` skips project settings files and `.mcp.json` entirely, including `env` and helpers, while preserving user settings. `--bare` does not block project `env` blocks and some helpers. |
| 4-{{option:d}} | `--bare` disables automatic discovery of hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, and `.mcp.json` servers in both home and project directories, eliminating those machine differences. |
| 5-{{option:e}} | These rules are unused in `-p` runs in untrusted folders, so no additional blocking is needed. |
| {{option:f}} unused | This real unattended-execution flag automatically denies requests needing approval, but does not disable repository-provided surfaces. |

questions.title: Per-tool approval policies for a hosted MCP payment server
questions.prompt:
A team connects a payment-service server through hosted MCP in the OpenAI Responses API. It exposes three tools:

- `get_invoice`: retrieves an invoice.
- `list_vendors`: retrieves a vendor list.
- `create_payment`: executes a transfer.

Lookup tools must run **without approval waits**, transfers require officer approval **on every call**, and transfer functionality **cannot be removed**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Set server `require_approval: "never"` for all three tools, instruct the model to ask the officer before transfers in the system prompt, and log calls.
Under `require_approval.never.tool_names`, list only `get_invoice` and `list_vendors` to exempt lookups; have the officer approve each `create_payment` approval request before continuing.
Set server `require_approval: "always"` so all calls, including lookups, return `mcp_approval_request`; have the officer approve each and log approvals in the application.
Remove `create_payment` from `allowed_tools` so the model never receives it; have the officer transfer funds in a separate UI while the agent only presents lookup results.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI documentation says hosted MCP requests approval by default before sending data to connectors or remote servers. `require_approval` supports `always`, `never`, or an object listing `tool_names` under `never` for per-tool exemptions. Requests arrive as `mcp_approval_request` and are answered through `mcp_approval_response`. Each approval covers one tool call only, so repeated calls require new approval. `allowed_tools` separately limits which tools are retrieved from the server. The decisive evidence is [no lookup waits], [approval per transfer call], and [retain transfer functionality], respectively eliminating {{option:C}}, {{option:A}}, and {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes waits but merely relies on model compliance rather than enforcing approval for every transfer, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: It keeps default approvals and exempts only lookups, requiring approval for every transfer. Officer response can become a bottleneck at high transfer volume; newly added server tools require approval by default, so new lookup tools require updating the exemption list.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is the safest option, but lookup approvals violate the first condition.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Withholding the transfer tool is safe, but violates the third condition requiring agent-executed transfers. Tool-exposure restrictions do not replace approval policy.

Additional point: Documentation recommends using only trusted remote MCP servers and warns that malicious servers can extract everything in model context. It also recommends reviewing and logging data sent to servers.

**References**: [MCP and Connectors › Approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Managed MCP settings balancing team autonomy and server-name spoofing
questions.prompt:
Security centrally controls MCP connections for 600 Claude Code developers. About 20 teams use internal remote HTTP and local stdio servers, with several new servers each quarter. Requirements:

- Unapproved servers **must remain blocked even if developers allow them in personal settings**.
- Unapproved servers **must not pass by reusing an approved server's name**.
- Teams must **add servers themselves within approved boundaries**, without security distributing a file for each team.
- Three security staff can process new-server registration requests, even if this takes several business days.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Define all approved servers in `managed-mcp.json` for exclusive control, updating and distributing the file to all developers for every new team-server request.
Populate managed `allowedMcpServers` with `serverName` entries and enable `allowManagedMcpServersOnly`, allowing only approved names and ignoring developer lists.
Populate managed `allowedMcpServers` with internal-domain `serverUrl` patterns and approved stdio `serverCommand` entries, enabling `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` to ignore developer allowlists.
Populate managed `allowedMcpServers` with internal-domain `serverUrl` patterns and approved stdio `serverCommand` entries, but omit `allowManagedMcpServersOnly` so developer allowlists merge.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code managed-MCP documentation says `serverName` matches only user-chosen labels and is not a security control. To constrain actual servers, use `serverCommand` or `serverUrl`. `serverUrl` supports wildcards; `serverCommand` requires exact command and argument matching, including order. Without `allowManagedMcpServersOnly`, allowlists from all scopes merge, letting developers expand access through personal settings; enabling it uses only managed allowlists. Denylists always take precedence. The decisive evidence is [personal settings cannot authorize access], [same-name unapproved servers blocked], and [teams add their own servers], respectively eliminating {{option:D}}, {{option:B}}, and {{option:A}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It blocks unapproved servers and name spoofing, but prevents team self-service and requires security to redistribute files, violating the third condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It ignores developer settings, but an unapproved server can pass by matching a name, violating the second condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Actual URLs and commands define the approved boundary, only managed lists count, and teams can add servers within it. Out-of-scope and new stdio servers require security entries; `serverCommand` matches arguments exactly and does not compare `env` values.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: URL/command criteria are appropriate, but merging lets developers authorize unapproved servers through their own entries, violating the first condition.

Additional point: If an allowlist contains any `serverUrl` entry, remote servers must match a URL entry; if it contains `serverCommand`, stdio servers must match a command entry. Name matching cannot qualify them in those cases.

**References**: [Control MCP server access for your organization › Match servers by URL, command, or name](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp) · [Control MCP server access for your organization › Restrict the allowlist to managed settings only](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp)

questions.title: Choosing where to enforce tenant isolation
questions.prompt: Considering [Requirement 1] and [Existing environment] together, which isolation method is **most appropriate**?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Serim Logistics handles deliveries and returns for 40 client companies. It has three developers and a separate two-person security team. Several clients join or leave each quarter.
>
> [Existing environment] The delivery-support agent uses Gemini and ADK. Client representatives authenticate through SSO and use chat to look up shipments and request refunds. The tools, `query_shipment(shipment_id)` and `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`, both call the logistics-system API through one service account. Shipment and order identifiers are sequential numbers without tenant information. The authenticated representative's `tenant_id` and `user_id` are stored in session state. Two or three tools are added each quarter. An internal messenger was introduced and the logo changed last quarter.
>
> [Requirement 1 — Tenant isolation] A representative's session must not access another tenant's shipment or refund data. Red-team testing reproduced hidden instructions in shipment notes causing the model to use another tenant's identifiers as arguments. Model-generated arguments are untrusted. The latency budget permits at most **one** logistics-system API call per tool invocation.
>
> [Requirement 2 — Refund authorization] Refund limits depend on the representative's tenant IdP group: KRW 500,000 for team members and KRW 5,000,000 for managers. Limits already exist in the tenant system and **must not be copied** into the agent app. Representatives expect immediate refund execution from chat requests and accept consent once on first use each day.
>
> [Security requirements] Every tool-call log must identify the requesting representative. Model output is untrusted, and these constraints must remain manageable for the three-person development team.

options.text: Have each tool read `tenant_id` from developer-controlled Tool Context and add it as a mandatory logistics-API query filter, returning an error if the model-provided identifier does not belong to that tenant.
Use a Before Tool Callback to query the logistics API for identifier ownership before each tool call; block mismatches with the session's `tenant_id` and execute the tool only if they match.
Instruct the model not to use identifiers outside the session's tenant and place a Model Armor plugin before it to filter injection in external text such as shipment notes.
Create a service account per tenant and have a Before Tool Callback select the account matching the session's `tenant_id`, limiting each account to its tenant's data.

questions.explanation:
ADK safety guidance explains that, unlike model-provided arguments, Tool Context is deterministically set by developers. In-tool guardrails can compare arguments against developer-defined policy and return errors for violations. Before Tool Callbacks can access agent state, tools, and arguments and block calls, but fail when information necessary to enforce policy is absent from arguments. The decisive evidence is Requirement 1's [do not trust model-generated arguments] and [one logistics-API call], plus the existing environment's [identifiers contain no tenant information]. These eliminate {{option:B}} and {{option:C}}; the three-person development team eliminates {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: A filter embedded in the query deterministically enforces isolation in one call without an extra lookup. Each tool needs filtering and ownership validation; shared helpers and tests are needed to prevent omissions as new tools arrive each quarter.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Identifiers lack tenant information, so the callback must first look it up, producing two calls and exceeding the latency budget. Its advantage is a generic approach without changing tools.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It is nondeterministic and relies on model judgment and input-detection accuracy, contrary to distrust of model arguments. Model Armor detects harmful input; it does not verify tenant ownership.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It deterministically isolates at the identity level, but provisioning and revoking accounts for 40 tenants as contracts change exceeds the three-person team's capacity.

Additional point: Service accounts and perimeter controls are coarse-grained. ADK likewise says finer restrictions belong to tool-level guardrails.

**References**: [Safety and Security for AI Agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Choosing the identity used by the refund tool
questions.prompt: Considering [Requirement 2] and [Security requirements] together, which identity approach is **most appropriate** for `issue_refund`?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Serim Logistics handles deliveries and returns for 40 client companies. It has three developers and a separate two-person security team. Several clients join or leave each quarter.
>
> [Existing environment] The delivery-support agent uses Gemini and ADK. Client representatives authenticate through SSO and use chat to look up shipments and request refunds. The tools, `query_shipment(shipment_id)` and `issue_refund(order_id, amount)`, both call the logistics-system API through one service account. Shipment and order identifiers are sequential numbers without tenant information. The authenticated representative's `tenant_id` and `user_id` are stored in session state. Two or three tools are added each quarter. An internal messenger was introduced and the logo changed last quarter.
>
> [Requirement 1 — Tenant isolation] A representative's session must not access another tenant's shipment or refund data. Red-team testing reproduced hidden instructions in shipment notes causing the model to use another tenant's identifiers as arguments. Model-generated arguments are untrusted. The latency budget permits at most **one** logistics-system API call per tool invocation.
>
> [Requirement 2 — Refund authorization] Refund limits depend on the representative's tenant IdP group: KRW 500,000 for team members and KRW 5,000,000 for managers. Limits already exist in the tenant system and **must not be copied** into the agent app. Representatives expect immediate refund execution from chat requests and accept consent once on first use each day.
>
> [Security requirements] Every tool-call log must identify the requesting representative. Model output is untrusted, and these constraints must remain manageable for the three-person development team.

options.text: Keep service-account Agent-Auth for `issue_refund`, copy member/manager limits into an application settings table, and compare limits inside the tool before calling. Log the requesting employee as an argument, reconcile the table quarterly, and retain service-account access for `query_shipment`.
Call `issue_refund` with the employee's OAuth User-Auth, requiring a separate consent screen for every refund and logging the confirmation. Use the same employee OAuth for `query_shipment`.

Restrict `issue_refund` to a read-only service account, requiring employees to execute refunds directly in the logistics UI while the agent only explains eligibility and limits. Keep `query_shipment` on a read-only service account.

Call `issue_refund` with employee OAuth User-Auth, obtaining consent once on first use and retaining it for the day. Let the tenant system enforce limits and record the employee in logs; keep `query_shipment` on a read-only service account.

questions.explanation:
ADK safety guidance identifies tool identity as a key security decision and allows different approaches per tool. Agent-Auth suits users with identical access and can use read-only permissions to prevent writes, but user attribution in logs needs separate handling. User-Auth lets external systems enforce the user's own permissions so the agent cannot exceed them; delegated OAuth scopes are often broader than needed, requiring additional constraints. The decisive evidence is Requirement 2's [IdP-group limits with no duplicate copy] and [immediate chat-request execution with once-daily consent], plus [requesting employee in call logs].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It executes immediately but duplicates limits in the app, violating the no-copy requirement. IdP-group changes can make the copy stale, and all calls appear under the service-account identity.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Permissions are appropriate, but consent screens on every refund violate immediate execution from chat.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Read-only identity is safest but violates the requirement for the agent to execute refunds.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: The external system enforces limits under the employee's identity, logs retain attribution, and lookups remain read-only. OAuth token storage and refresh require management, initial daily consent adds friction, and broad delegated scopes may require separate confirmation for high-value refunds.

Additional point: The internal-messenger rollout and logo change in the existing environment are distractors unrelated to tool identity.

**References**: [Safety and Security for AI Agents (ADK)](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Combining web and internal-document search for a ZDR clinical assistant
questions.prompt:
A general hospital is building a clinical-query assistant with the OpenAI Responses API. It has a ZDR agreement and uses an API key from a ZDR-enabled project. Queries may contain patient information, so legal requires using web search only in a BAA-covered configuration. Constraints:

- Reference external clinical guidelines through the **web search tool**, without building a custom collection infrastructure.
- About **600 internal protocol PDFs** are not on the public web and need **separate search**.
- Under the ZDR agreement, do not use **endpoints that retain customer content as application state**.
- Use web search only in a **BAA-covered** configuration.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Do not use web search; download external guidelines in advance and index them alongside internal protocols. Use the embeddings endpoint with a self-hosted vector database, passing retrieved results into Responses.

Set web search to `external_web_access: false` for external guidelines. Index internal protocols with the embeddings endpoint, retrieve from a self-hosted vector database, and pass results into Responses.
Use web search with live internet access for external guidelines. Index internal protocols with the embeddings endpoint, retrieve from a self-hosted vector database, and pass results into Responses.
Set web search to `external_web_access: false` for external guidelines. Upload internal protocols through Files, create a vector store, and search with `file_search`.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI data-controls documentation says web search with live internet access is not HIPAA eligible or covered by a BAA. Offline/cache-only mode (`external_web_access: false`) can be BAA-covered when using a ZDR-project key within a ZDR organization; this guidance applies only to the Responses API's `web_search` tool. Responses and embeddings are ZDR-eligible, while vector stores and Files are ineligible and retain application state until deletion. The decisive evidence is [BAA-covered web search only], [no endpoints retaining application state], and [web search for external guidelines, separate search for internal protocols].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It uses only ZDR-eligible endpoints, but creates a custom external-guideline collection infrastructure instead of using web search.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Web search uses a BAA-covered mode, while internal search uses eligible endpoints and hospital-controlled storage. It sacrifices live internet access and requires the hospital to update and operate embedding indexes and the vector database.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Internal search is appropriate, but live-internet web search is not BAA-covered and cannot be used for potentially patient-bearing queries.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The web-search mode is appropriate, but Files and vector stores are not ZDR-eligible; retaining the 600 protocols as application state violates the agreement.

**References**: [Data controls in the OpenAI platform › Web Search, Zero Data Retention](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data)

questions.title: Ordering PDF analysis and deletion through the Files API
questions.prompt:
A server analyzes customer-submitted PDFs using the Claude API. Each document is used only once, and security wants to minimize its residence in the Files API. Arrange these steps by dependency.

(1) Receive the response and confirm the analysis request has completed. (2) Delete the file through the deletion endpoint. (3) Upload the file with an expiry (`expires_in_seconds`) and receive its `id`. (4) Send a Messages request with that `id` as `file_id` in a document block.

items.text: Receive the response and confirm the analysis request has completed.
Delete the file through the deletion endpoint.
Upload the file with an expiry (`expires_in_seconds`) and receive its `id`.
Send a Messages request with that `id` as `file_id` in a document block.

questions.explanation:
Files API documentation says to reference the upload response's `id` as `file_id` in a Messages document block. Files remain until deletion or `expires_at`; expiry is enabled only when specified during upload. Deleted files cannot be recovered, and active Messages calls may retain access immediately after deletion. Each step supplies an input needed by the next.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Upload with expiry and receive `id` | None. This creates the ID used later and the expiry setting, which must be set at upload. | Expiry is enabled only by supplying `expires_in_seconds` at upload; otherwise `expires_at` is `null`. |
| 2 | (4) Make the Messages request using `file_id` | The ID is needed to construct the document block. | Reference the upload response's `id` as `file_id`. |
| 3 | (1) Receive the response and confirm completion | A request must precede its response. | Active calls may retain file access after deletion, so confirm completion before deleting. |
| 4 | (2) Delete | Confirm analysis is complete and no further use remains; deletion is irreversible. | Delete through `DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}`; deleted files cannot be recovered. |

Additional point: Uploaded files are accessible workspace-wide, so do not trust end-user-supplied `file_id` values. Uploaded files cannot be downloaded again. Files API is not ZDR-eligible.

**References**: [Files API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files) · [API and data retention › Feature eligibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention)

questions.title: ZDR counseling agents and the retention scope of Managed Agents
questions.prompt:
Medical-counseling provider NuriCare has a Claude API ZDR agreement. It has two agents:

- New patient-counseling agent: conversations and tool results contain medical information; sessions pause and resume days later. It uses client-side bash and text-editing tools.
- Existing developer-support agent: answers internal code questions, already runs on Claude Managed Agents, and handles no medical information.

Requirements:

- Prompts, responses, and session records containing medical information **must not persist at Anthropic outside ZDR coverage**.
- The patient agent must support **session pause and resume**.
- The developer agent must continue **unchanged without rework**.
- The two-person platform team should add only necessary components.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Build the patient agent with Managed Agents using a self-hosted sandbox on company infrastructure; delete sessions through the API after counseling and leave the developer agent unchanged.

Build the patient agent as a custom Messages API loop, uploading patient documents through Files and referencing `file_id`; keep session state in the app database, delete analyzed documents, and leave the developer agent unchanged.

Build only the patient agent as a custom Messages API loop with client-side bash and text editing, retaining documents and session state in company storage; keep the developer agent on Managed Agents.
Migrate both agents to custom Messages API loops and stop using Managed Agents so every organizational agent uses the same ZDR-eligible features under one management approach.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's retention documentation classifies Claude Managed Agents as ZDR-ineligible: sessions are stateful resources whose records persist until deletion, including all subfeatures such as self-hosted sandboxes. Messages API and client-side bash and text-editing tools are eligible; Files API is not. The Managed Agents overview likewise says server-stored session history is outside ZDR and HIPAA BAA coverage and recommends Messages API for custom agent loops. The decisive evidence is [medical information must remain within ZDR], [no rework of the existing agent], and [minimal new components], eliminating {{option:A}} and {{option:B}}, then {{option:D}}.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Company-hosted execution and eventual deletion do not change the fact that all Managed Agents, including self-hosted sandboxes, are ineligible and retain session history server-side until deletion. This violates the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The Messages loop is eligible, but Files API retains documents at Anthropic until deletion or expiry and is ineligible, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: Medical information uses only eligible features while the existing agent remains intact. The team must implement and operate the agent loop and session store, manage database retention and deletion, and support two approaches concurrently.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Uniform eligibility simplifies the architecture but rebuilding the existing developer agent violates the third condition and staffing constraint.

Additional point: Documentation says reported conversations or sessions may be retained for up to two years even in ZDR organizations, and Covered Models such as Fable 5.1 require 30-day retention.

**References**: [API and data retention › What ZDR does not cover](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention) · [API and data retention › Feature eligibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention) · [Claude Managed Agents overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview)

questions.title: Storing and restricting Gemini API keys on servers
questions.prompt:
An internal backend calls the Gemini API through two fixed public NAT IP addresses. Key management has not yet been defined, so security is choosing storage and restrictions. Requirements:

- Keys **must not appear in source repositories or configuration files**.
- Even if leaked, calls **from outside designated servers must be rejected**.
- Quarterly rotation must require **no container-image rebuild or code change**.

According to Gemini API documentation, which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Restrict the key to Gemini API without IP restrictions, store it in a CI secret variable, and embed it in the container image at build time. Configure billing alerts.
Restrict the key to Gemini API and the two NAT IPs, store it in Secret Manager, and load it through an environment variable at service startup. Configure billing alerts.
Restrict the key to Gemini API and the two NAT IPs, commit it in an encrypted configuration file, and decrypt during deployment. Configure billing alerts.
Restrict the key to Gemini API without IP restrictions, store it in Secret Manager, and load it through an environment variable at startup. Configure billing alerts.

questions.explanation:
Gemini API-key documentation recommends keeping keys out of source control, reading them through environment variables, and using a production secret store such as Google Cloud Secret Manager. Restrictions reduce the impact of exposure: AI Studio can restrict a key to Gemini API, and application restrictions can allow specific IPs. Billing alerts notify usage or cost spikes. The decisive evidence is [no keys in repositories/configuration files], [reject outside-server calls], and [no rebuild/code changes on rotation], respectively eliminating {{option:C}}, {{option:D}}, and {{option:A}}; {{option:A}} also violates the second condition.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Embedding the key requires rebuilding each quarter, and absent IP restrictions permit calls elsewhere.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Startup retrieval from a secret store avoids rebuilds; allowed IPs reject external callers, and API-specific restriction reduces impact. Secret Manager permissions need management, instances must restart to load rotated keys, and NAT changes require updating allowed IPs.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Restrictions are appropriate, but even encrypted keys are committed to source control, violating the first condition and documentation guidance.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Storage and rotation are appropriate, but a leaked key works outside designated servers without IP restrictions, violating the second condition.

Additional point: Rotation sequencing after exposure—do not delete the old key before verifying the new one—is covered in incident response, not this question.

**References**: [Using Gemini API keys](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/api-key)

questions.title: Correcting two errors in a report claiming all Claude Code use is covered by ZDR
questions.prompt:
Of 300 Claude Code developers, about 40 use personal Claude Pro accounts on work repositories and about 30 call models through third-party IDE extensions or code-review services. The rest use the organization's commercial API key. Security reports that all Claude Code use is within ZDR because the organization has an Anthropic ZDR agreement. Constraints:

- Claude Code is essential and **cannot be banned**.
- Usage statistics are needed for security audits, so **telemetry cannot be disabled**.
- Customer source code must not leave ZDR coverage.

Select **two corrective actions**.

options.text: Disable usage-statistics transmission to remove the ZDR exception for API-key-based Claude Code.
Assign organizational Claude Teams seats to personal Pro users so they sign into the same Claude Code with organization accounts, with administrators managing seat usage.
Require Claude Code authentication with the organization's commercial API key on work repositories, prohibiting personal-subscription login for that work.
Switch developers to pasting code and asking questions in the Console playground.
Separate third-party-mediated usage from the Anthropic ZDR report and register it for independent review and approval of vendor data-handling terms.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic retention documentation limits Claude Code ZDR coverage to use with a commercial organization's API key. Even then, usage statistics may be retained outside ZDR if metrics logging is enabled. Exclusions include Console and playground, consumer Free/Pro/Max plans including Claude Code used through them, Teams/Enterprise product interfaces (Enterprise Claude Code requires a separate agreement), and third-party integrations. The decisive evidence is [cannot ban Claude Code], [telemetry required], and [customer source must remain within ZDR].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It removes the documented statistics exception but violates required telemetry and does not address personal accounts or third parties.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Accounts become organizational, but Teams product interfaces are ineligible, leaving source outside ZDR.
- **{{option:C}} (correct)**: It moves consumer-plan use onto a covered authentication path. Developers lose personal-subscription convenience, and organizational key issuance and management increase.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Console/playground is outside ZDR and does not replace the Claude Code workflow.
- **{{option:E}} (correct)**: Anthropic ZDR does not cover third-party processing, so separate reporting and evaluation/approval are required. Vendor-by-vendor reviews add work, and some services may need to be discontinued.

Additional point: ZDR must be enabled separately for each organization, and reported conversations may be retained for up to two years regardless of the agreement.

**References**: [API and data retention › What ZDR covers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention) · [API and data retention › What ZDR does not cover](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention)

questions.title: Choosing validation that prevents sensitive data from persisting in file-based memory
questions.prompt:
A fintech counseling agent uses Claude's `memory` tool to store customer preferences and ongoing case state under `/memories`. The tool is client-side, so the team's handler performs file reads and writes. Customers sometimes paste card numbers or API keys into conversations, and security is choosing where to prevent these values from entering memory. Constraints:

- **Cross-session continuity** is required. Memory needs roughly ten preference fields, such as language, contact time, and product interests, plus case stage; each value comes from predefined choices.
- Card numbers and keys **must never reach disk**. Later deletion is unacceptable, as is retaining values that evade known-format patterns.
- **No extra model calls on memory writes** are possible because the latency budget is exhausted.
- Counselors prefer free-text notes preserving customer context, but these are optional.

Which design is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Immediately before writing, scan for card-number and key patterns, masking or rejecting matches and returning errors to the model. Store other free-text notes unchanged.
Allow writes only for predefined field names and choices, reject free text, and return an error plus allowed choices to the model when rejected.
Classify every write with a separate small-model call, block sensitive content, and log classifications and rationales for audit.
Write whatever the model requests, then scan all `/memories` files nightly with patterns to delete sensitive lines and log deletions.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's memory documentation says Claude usually refuses to write sensitive information, but stronger guarantees require handler-side validation before files are written. Because the handler executes all file operations, these safeguards are the developer's responsibility. The decisive evidence is [never reaches disk], [no extra model calls], and [predefined choices for field values]. Allowlist validation reconciles continuity with nonpersistence by eliminating the possibility of arbitrary values evading patterns. The correct answer sacrifices free-text notes.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Free text plus known-pattern filtering allows unrecognized key formats or altered numbers through, so it cannot guarantee nonpersistence. It does preserve counselors' preferred notes.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Before writing, deterministic field-name/value allowlisting prevents out-of-list values from reaching disk without extra model calls. Free-text notes are lost, and each new preference field or choice requires an allowlist update.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Contextual classification is useful, but extra write-path model calls violate the latency constraint, and probabilistic decisions can still let values through.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Continuity and free text are retained, but values remain on disk until the nightly batch; retrospective deletion is explicitly unacceptable.

Additional point: Path validation preventing access outside `/memories`, file-size limits, and expiry of stale files are separate handler responsibilities in the same documentation.

**References**: [Memory tool › Security considerations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool)

questions.title: Selecting content-collection variables
questions.prompt: Which content-collection configuration should be **fixed in the managed settings `env` block** to satisfy [Requirements 1–3]?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Daon Software deployed Claude Code to 300 developers. Four security staff operate an OpenTelemetry collector, and developers use the CLI on their laptops. Managed settings can be distributed to all laptops.
>
> [Existing environment] Telemetry is enabled with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` and sent through OTLP to an internal collector. Developers currently set their own `OTEL_*` variables in shell profiles and project settings; some have disabled log export, and some repositories have specified different endpoints. An internal-wiki migration finishes this quarter.
>
> [Requirement 1 — Forensics] After an incident, reconstruct which shell commands executed.
>
> [Requirement 2 — Prohibited collection] **Do not collect** raw prompts or source code, including tool outputs. Mask secret patterns in command text at the collector.
>
> [Requirement 3 — Tamper resistance] **Lock collection destinations and content through managed settings** so developer or repository settings cannot alter or disable them.
>
> [Requirement 4 — Autonomy and audit] Organizational policy lets developers choose permission modes, including auto mode. Security needs central visibility into permanent permission approvals and permission-mode changes.

options.text: Set managed `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` and explicitly disable tool-output, prompt, and raw-body variables. Mask command text at the collector.
Set managed `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1`, leaving other content variables at their default disabled values. Mask command text at the collector.
Explicitly disable all content-collection variables in managed `env`, using tool allow/deny decision events and usage metrics for incident investigations.
Set managed `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` and `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1`, explicitly disabling prompt and raw-body variables. Mask source-code patterns in tool output at the collector.

questions.explanation:
Claude Code content-collection variables default to off. `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS` records Bash commands, MCP server/tool names, and tool inputs; `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT` records tool outputs; `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS` records raw prompts; `OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES` includes full conversation history in bodies. Managed `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*` settings remove conflicting developer variables, but control delivery rather than collected content. To lock content, explicitly set `OTEL_LOG_*` values in managed settings too. The decisive evidence is Requirement 1's command reconstruction, Requirement 2's ban on prompt/source collection, and Requirement 3's fixed collection scope. The correct approach accepts truncation of tool-input values longer than the documented 512 characters and ongoing masking-rule maintenance.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Enable command details and explicitly disable the rest, reducing developers' ability to broaden collection through their environment. Long commands may be truncated, limiting reconstruction, and collector secret-masking rules require maintenance.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Current content satisfies Requirements 1 and 2, but unspecified variables are not locked and developers can enable them, violating Requirement 3. It has the lowest administration burden.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It locks content most tightly, but decision events lack command text, which requires tool-detail logging, so Requirement 1 is unmet.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Tool output can include source files read or edited, so collecting it violates Requirement 2 even if the collector later masks it. It provides the richest reconstruction.

Additional point: The internal-wiki migration is irrelevant distractor information.

**References**: [Monitoring › Content-logging variables](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) · [Monitoring › Locking telemetry with managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage)

questions.title: Designing tamper resistance and audit signals
questions.prompt: Which configuration **best addresses** the tampering in [Existing environment] while satisfying [Requirements 3–4]?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Daon Software deployed Claude Code to 300 developers. Four security staff operate an OpenTelemetry collector, and developers use the CLI on their laptops. Managed settings can be distributed to all laptops.
>
> [Existing environment] Telemetry is enabled with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` and sent through OTLP to an internal collector. Developers currently set their own `OTEL_*` variables in shell profiles and project settings; some have disabled log export, and some repositories have specified different endpoints. An internal-wiki migration finishes this quarter.
>
> [Requirement 1 — Forensics] After an incident, reconstruct which shell commands executed.
>
> [Requirement 2 — Prohibited collection] **Do not collect** raw prompts or source code, including tool outputs. Mask secret patterns in command text at the collector.
>
> [Requirement 3 — Tamper resistance] **Lock collection destinations and content through managed settings** so developer or repository settings cannot alter or disable them.
>
> [Requirement 4 — Autonomy and audit] Organizational policy lets developers choose permission modes, including auto mode. Security needs central visibility into permanent permission approvals and permission-mode changes.

options.text: Lock OTLP endpoint, protocol, and headers in managed settings and alert on permission-mode changes and permanent approvals. Leave exporter-selection variables to developers.

Lock endpoint/headers, exporter selection (`OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER`, `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER`), and content variables in managed settings; use mode changes and `user_permanent` approvals as review signals without blocking them.
Set managed `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` and `permissions.disableAutoMode` to `"disable"` to prevent risky mode changes, leaving collection variables to developers.

Lock endpoint/headers and exporter selection in managed settings, alerting only on permanent approvals (`tool_decision` with `source: user_permanent`). Look up mode changes in session records when needed.

questions.explanation:
Documentation says managed endpoint, protocol, and credential variables remove conflicting developer variables, but exporter selectors (`OTEL_*_EXPORTER`) follow ordinary per-key precedence and must be explicitly managed to lock them. Repository settings cannot configure telemetry, but if managed settings or the execution environment do not specify a signal, a repository can disable it with `none`. Audit signals include `permission_mode_changed` (`from_mode`, `to_mode`, `trigger`) and `tool_decision` events with `source: user_permanent`. The decisive evidence is prior log-disabling, Requirement 3's locking, and Requirement 4's autonomy plus central visibility. Since the correct design does not block actions, it incurs false-positive review and retrospective-response work. In the interactive CLI, subsequent matching approvals are reported as `config`, so only the initial permanent approval produces that signal.

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Signals are appropriate, but unlocked exporter selectors allow logging to be disabled, eliminating audit events and violating Requirement 3.
- **{{option:B}} (correct)**: Managed destination, exporter selection, and content settings plus both review signals preserve autonomy.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Mode disabling works as a control but removes the autonomy required by Requirement 4, including auto mode, and does not prevent collection tampering.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Locking is appropriate, but it omits central visibility of mode changes, half of Requirement 4. Session records reside on developer laptops and are not central visibility.

**References**: [Monitoring › Events relevant to permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) · [Monitoring › Locking telemetry with managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage) · [Permissions › Managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)

questions.title: Allowing a retention-required model only for research in a ZDR organization
questions.prompt:
A fintech company operates a counseling-summary service in `support-prod` within a Claude API ZDR organization. Contractually, its prompts and responses must not be stored. Research wants a Covered Model requiring 30-day retention for a document-analysis tool using only public material, without customer data. Requirements:

- **Preserve ZDR** for counseling summaries.
- Research **must use the Covered Model**.
- Manage billing and administrator permissions within **the existing single organization**.

Which configuration is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Terminate organizational ZDR and switch everything to standard retention so both services can use the Covered Model, retaining current billing and administration.
Create a new research organization for the Covered Model, leaving counseling unchanged but managing billing and administrator accounts separately.
Build research in a dedicated workspace in the existing organization using a ZDR-eligible model, preserving ZDR but abandoning the Covered Model.
Create a dedicated research workspace in the same organization and enable Standard data retention only there to use the Covered Model.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic retention documentation says ZDR applies per organization and does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account. Covered Models require 30-day retention and cannot use ZDR without special approval. A ZDR organization can enable standard retention for one workspace to use them. This requires selecting the workspace in privacy settings and accepting terms; it is unavailable for Default Workspace. The decisive evidence is [preserve ZDR], [use Covered Model], and [one existing organization].

- **{{option:A}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Both services can use the model, but ending the agreement removes counseling ZDR, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Organizational separation preserves counseling ZDR but violates single-organization billing and administration.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: ZDR and organizational structure remain, but the required Covered Model is abandoned.
- **{{option:D}} (correct)**: It leaves `support-prod` untouched and enables retention only in the new workspace. That workspace's inputs and outputs are retained for 30 days, and flagged conversations may be retained for up to two years, requiring operational controls to exclude customer data from research input.

**References**: [API and data retention › Zero data retention, Policy exceptions, How to enable](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention)

questions.title: Protecting a voice assistant's Live API connection without a server proxy
questions.prompt:
A mobile voice assistant connects directly to Gemini Live API through WebSocket. There is no budget for a server proxy, and long-lived API keys in the app are prohibited. The backend can only issue ephemeral tokens to authenticated users. Requirements:

- Conversations last **up to 50 minutes**, and **context must survive interruptions**.
- A stolen token must permit **only the specified model/settings and only one new session**.
- One person must be able to maintain reconnection logic.

Which token-issuance approach is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Keep the default token expiry of 30 minutes for messaging, then obtain a new token and start a new session. Bind model/settings and refresh just before expiry.
Set `uses` to 1, extend `expireTime` to at least 50 minutes, bind the model and `sessionResumption` through `liveConnectConstraints`, and reconnect with the same token.
