questions.title: Application controls preventing one user from exhausting shared OpenAI limits
questions.prompt:
A B2B document-summarization SaaS sends all tenants' requests through one OpenAI project key. A user in one tenant floods it with scripted requests, exhausting shared limits and causing 429s for other users in the same tenant. Requirements:

- **Other users in the same tenant must be protected**.
- Quota-system identity storage must contain **only internal user IDs**.
- Some tenants need bulk processing, so **the feature cannot be disabled globally**.

Which control is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Enforce per-user periodic quotas and tenant-level caps in the application, applying hard caps or manual review to over-limit users and enabling bulk processing only for trusted tenants.
Strengthen exponential-backoff and jitter retries on 429s, increase retry counts to improve success, and follow `Retry-After`.
Create separate OpenAI projects and keys per tenant, without distinguishing users within each tenant, and monitor only project limits.
Temporarily block all requests from a tenant when flooding is detected, restoring access after a sales representative investigates.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI documents rate limits at organization and project levels, not user level. Applications should enforce daily, weekly, or monthly per-user limits, apply hard caps or manual review to excess usage, and reserve programmatic access or bulk processing for trusted customers. Failed requests also count toward per-minute limits. The decisive evidence is [protect other users in the same tenant], [minimal identifying information], and [retain bulk functionality]. The correct approach requires designing and operating quota values and may inconvenience legitimate high-volume users.

- **{{option:A}} (correct)**: Application-enforced user quotas and tenant caps satisfy all three requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: More retries do not restore exhausted limits, and failed attempts count toward per-minute limits, prolonging other users' 429s.
- **{{option:C}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It isolates tenants, but users within the same tenant still share limits with the flooding user.
- **{{option:D}} (incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Flooding stops, but legitimate users and bulk functionality are blocked for the entire tenant.

**References**: [Rate limits › Protecting shared limits and preventing abuse](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits)

questions.title: Updating a threat model when a new feature changes the attack surface and trust boundaries
questions.prompt: Hanbit Accounting has already documented a threat model for its internal policy Q&A chatbot. Its architecture diagram includes employee browsers, the chatbot server, an internal policy document repository, and the model API. It shows two trust boundaries: between the internet and the internal network, and between the chatbot server and the model API. This quarter, it is adding a feature in which the chatbot server fetches a web page from a URL pasted by an employee and compares it with company policy. A security officer wants to update the threat model before launch. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat the page as having the same trust level as the employee because the employee selected the URL, leave the diagram unchanged, and add only a standard web-vulnerability review of the new code.
Because an attack surface is a list of externally exposed ports and API endpoints, there is nothing to update if the feature creates no new endpoint.

Add the web-page body as a new input path and draw a new trust boundary where externally authored content enters the model context. Then identify threats along flows crossing it—indirect injection, internal access through server URL requests, and sending results outside—and determine mitigations.
Treat the threat model as a one-time initial-design document and add threats as they are discovered by red teaming after launch.

questions.explanation:
Threat modeling asks four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, how will we respond, and have we done enough? Trust boundaries in data-flow diagrams are key inputs showing where attacks can occur. The attack surface encompasses every point where an attacker can enter a system—in other words, all data and command paths entering and leaving an application—and changes to it require renewed threat modeling. In LLM applications, retrieved documents, web pages, and tool results are all attack surfaces alongside user input. The decisive evidence is [fetching web pages to compare with policy] and [only two trust boundaries].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: An employee selected the URL, but a third party authored the page. Trust depends on the content's author, so this body cannot be assigned the same trust as employee input.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The attack surface includes all data paths, not just exposed endpoints. Even without another endpoint, there is a new input path into model context.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It follows standard threat-modeling procedure: inventory the new input path, redraw the trust boundary, then identify threats for each flow crossing it.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: Red teaming tests implemented defenses. It cannot replace design-stage threat identification, and delaying until after launch exposes the already-open surface.

Further notes: Because the URL-fetching feature makes the server request a user-supplied address, it also introduces server-side request forgery (SSRF) risk (see SES-N8).

**Sources**: Industry-standard documentation (vendor-neutral) · [OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Threat_Modeling_Cheat_Sheet.html) (four questions, data-flow diagrams, and trust boundaries) · [OWASP Attack Surface Analysis Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Attack_Surface_Analysis_Cheat_Sheet.html) ("changes to the Attack Surface should trigger threat modeling")

questions.title: Adopting a model from a public hub
questions.prompt: Haneul Precision's AI team found an open-weight model on a public model hub for its internal document classifier. The publisher is an individual account, and the model page claims "highest score on internal benchmarks." The team rule is: "External components must have their provenance and integrity verified and may enter production only in a form reproducible internally." Which adoption procedure is most appropriate?

options.text: Because it has the highest benchmark score, download the latest hub version whenever the production server starts to automatically incorporate the publisher's updates.

Review the publisher and license, verify the weight-file hash and signature if available, pin a specific version, and retain it in an internal repository. Use only that copy in production, record it in the AI BOM, and approve it after evaluation on company documents.
Treat sufficiently high download counts and ratings as trustworthy and require only an antivirus scan before production.
Treat every external model as dangerous, never use one, and pretrain all models internally from scratch.

questions.explanation:
OWASP describes LLM supply-chain risk as systems being affected by tampering or contamination of external components such as third-party models, packages, adapters, and data. Public models may have weak provenance guarantees and hidden backdoors or malicious capabilities. Benchmark scores can be manipulated and cannot establish safety alone. Recommended controls include supplier review, maintaining signed component inventories (SBOMs and AI BOMs), verifying integrity through hashes and signatures, red-team evaluation on company-specific use cases before adoption, version management, and patching. The decisive evidence is [individual publisher], [only benchmark scores presented], and [internally reproducible form].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Fetching the latest version each time introduces unverified files into production; a compromised publisher account could directly deploy tampered versions. It also violates reproducibility.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It combines provenance review, integrity checks, version pinning, internal retention, component inventory, and company-specific evaluation. The tradeoff is slower updates because revalidation is required.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: Download counts and ratings do not guarantee provenance or integrity. Antivirus scans cannot verify behavior hidden in model weights.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: The recommendation is to validate external components before use, not prohibit them entirely. Pretraining from scratch for one document classifier is incompatible with reasonable cost and schedule.

Further notes: This risk is not limited to models. Dependency packages, adapters, and external tool servers require the same provenance and version management.

**Sources**: Industry-standard documentation (vendor-neutral) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 › LLM03: Supply Chain](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm032025-supply-chain/)

questions.title: Matching security-review findings to threat names
questions.prompt: For each finding in a security review of a production agent, select the most appropriate threat name on the right. Two options on the right are unused.

options.text: Excessive Agency
Data Exfiltration
Indirect Prompt Injection
Privilege Escalation
Prompt Leakage
Denial of Wallet

items.text: A procurement agent only needs to look up purchase orders, but for development convenience it was also given order-deletion and supplier-bank-account modification tools plus a write-enabled account from the outset. When it misinterpreted an ambiguous request, a supplier bank account was actually changed.

Network logs show that while an agent reading internal documents generated a response, it sent a request to an external-domain address carrying part of the document content. Internal data left the organization.
An externally operated MCP search server returns normal search results with instructions addressed to the agent mixed into the response body. Otherwise, it behaves like a normal tool.
An agent that started with a read-only role used a role-configuration tool to expand its own permissions and execute administrator-only functions.

questions.explanation:
All four findings describe real problems, but the central defect differs. OWASP defines Excessive Agency as a vulnerability enabling harmful actions in response to ambiguous or manipulated LLM outputs, with causes divided into excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy. Indirect Prompt Injection occurs when an LLM accepts external input such as a website or file and embedded instructions alter model behavior. Tool-server responses also enter context on every call; finding 3 therefore describes indirect injection targeting the agent through instructions embedded in a response. The decisive evidence is each finding's key phrase.

| Number | Answer | Key phrase |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:a}}. Excessive Agency | [provided from the outset], [misinterpreted an ambiguous request]. Unnecessary functions and write permissions were granted at design time. |
| 2 | {{option:b}}. Data Exfiltration | [left the organization]. Regardless of the causal path, the outcome is data being sent outside. |
| 3 | {{option:c}}. Indirect Prompt Injection | [instructions embedded in the response body]. The contaminated surface is the tool response. |
| 4 | {{option:d}}. Privilege Escalation | [expanded its own permissions]. It obtained higher privileges than assigned. |

- **{{option:e}}. Prompt Leakage (Unused)**: This exposes system-prompt content to users. None of the four findings involves prompt disclosure.
- **{{option:f}}. Denial of Wallet (Unused)**: This exhausts funds through excessive calls. The findings concern permissions and data rather than cost.

Further notes: Row 1 is a design problem involving overly broad permissions from the outset; row 4 is a dynamic problem of obtaining more permissions than assigned. Both defenses converge on complete mediation: each tool checks the requesting actor's permissions at invocation time.

**Sources**: Industry-standard documentation (vendor-neutral) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 › LLM06: Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 › LLM01: Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) (verified wording: "Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files.") · [MCP Security Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices) (uses Data Exfiltration and Privilege Escalation as risk categories).

questions.title: Splitting a general-purpose SQL tool into task-specific tools
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics' operations-support agent reads and modifies its production database through one tool, run_sql, using an administrator database account. It has only three duties: (1) look up order status, (2) look up shipping addresses, and (3) mark an order "refund pending." Red teaming found that successful indirect injection would let it read or delete any table, making the blast radius the entire database. The conditions are:

- The agent must continue performing all three duties.
- Implement within this quarter.
- Do not increase model calls per request.

Which change most reduces the blast radius?

options.text: Tell the model in its system prompt not to use DROP, DELETE, or TRUNCATE and add a string check before the tool that blocks queries containing those words.
Keep run_sql but add a second model call before execution to assess danger and execute only approved queries.
Keep run_sql but make the database account read-only. Have staff mark refunds pending manually in the UI.

Remove run_sql and replace it with get_order_status(order_id), get_shipping_address(order_id), and mark_refund_pending(order_id). Each tool binds arguments to a fixed query, and its database account has only read access to required columns and UPDATE permission on the single status column.

questions.explanation:
OWASP divides Excessive Agency into excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy. Its mitigations recommend granular tools instead of open-ended extensions, minimizing tool functions and downstream permissions, and enforcing authorization in downstream systems through complete mediation. This exam calls narrowing callable actions and arguments to business-task scope Action Scoping. The decisive evidence is [one run_sql tool with administrator privileges], [the agent must continue all three duties], and [no additional model calls]; these conditions rule out A, B, and C respectively.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: A word denylist does not reduce permissions. Other queries with equivalent effects and unrestricted reads remain available, leaving the blast radius unchanged.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: The judgment is nondeterministic and adds a model call per request. Administrator privileges remain, so one incorrect judgment exposes the whole database.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Write risk decreases, but all-table read access remains and the agent no longer performs the third duty as required.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It narrows functions (three actions), arguments (order_id), and permissions (required columns and one column's UPDATE) to task scope. Even successful injection is limited to those actions. The tradeoff is adding tools and permissions whenever new duties arise.

Further notes: Each tool must also verify that the order belongs to the requesting customer's account to prevent access to another customer's order (see the Serim Logistics case, Q57).

**Sources**: Industry-standard documentation (vendor-neutral) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 › LLM06: Excessive Agency › Prevention](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) · Action Scoping and Blast Radius follow this exam's glossary definitions

questions.title: Keeping an agent’s tool credentials outside the model
questions.prompt:
Mirae Trading's internal agent calls its inventory API. The current implementation places a developer's personal API token in the system prompt and has the model insert it into a header field in tool arguments. Security notes that successful indirect injection could cause the model to send the token outside, and the token also appears in conversation logs and traces. Requirements are:

- Inventory API audit logs must identify "this agent," not an individual, as the caller.
- The agent must keep working even if the developer leaves.
- The change must be implementable this quarter.

Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Create a dedicated service account for the agent with inventory-read permission only and store its key in a secrets-management service. Only the tool-executing backend reads the key and adds the authentication header; the model produces nonsecret arguments such as item codes. Rotate the key periodically and audit access records.
Move the token out of the system prompt and into the start of the user's first message so any leak affects only that conversation.
Keep the developer's personal token but reduce rotation to every 90 days. Document its location for handover when the developer leaves.
Create one shared administrator service account for all internal agents, store its key in an environment variable, and inject the same value into every agent container.

questions.explanation:
Credentials should be kept where the model cannot see them (Credential Isolation), because values in model context can escape through injection or logs. General Secret Management principles are to centralize secrets in a secrets-management service, keep plaintext secrets out of source code, prompts, and logs, restrict access with least privilege, rotate periodically, and audit reads. Automated actors should use dedicated Service Accounts rather than human accounts, with only required permissions. The decisive evidence is [personal token in the system prompt], [caller must be identified as this agent], and [must not stop when the developer leaves].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It removes the key from model context, separates identity through a dedicated service account, minimizes permissions, and adds rotation and auditing. The tradeoff is implementing secrets-service integration and automated key rotation.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: The token remains in model context, preserving injection and logging exposure, and remains a personal token.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Personal tokens identify the individual in audit logs and risk disruption on departure; the token also remains in model context. Shorter rotation does not fix the architecture.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: A shared administrator key expands the blast radius to all agents and internal APIs and prevents distinguishing agents in logs. Its permissions far exceed what is necessary.

Further notes: If the key is already exposed in a public repository or elsewhere, immediate deactivation and rotation are containment priorities separate from this architectural improvement (see Q80 and Q81).

**Sources**: Industry-standard documentation (vendor-neutral) · [OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html) (centralized management, least privilege, rotation, auditing, no plaintext logging, dedicated CI/CD service accounts) · [OWASP LLM06: Excessive Agency › Prevention](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)

questions.title: Skipped consent in an MCP proxy using a static client ID
questions.prompt: Haneul Precision's platform team operates an internal MCP proxy connecting to an external SaaS API. It always connects to the SaaS authorization server with the same static client ID and permits dynamic registration of MCP clients. Once a user approves, the SaaS authorization server leaves a consent cookie in the browser and skips later consent screens. Security review notes that a previously approved user's browser might also skip consent for a different client registered later, creating a confused deputy problem. Which change most directly reduces the risk?

options.text: Extend the SaaS authorization server's consent-cookie lifetime so users do not repeatedly see the same consent screen.

Have the proxy keep a server-side list of approved client_id values per user and require its own consent screen before entering the SaaS authorization flow, showing the requesting client name, requested scopes, and registered redirect_uri. Permit redirect_uri only when it exactly matches the registered value.
Relax redirect_uri validation to domain-suffix pattern matching to reduce registration rejections for legitimate clients.
Eliminate the proxy's token-issuance stage by passing tokens supplied by dynamically registered clients directly to the SaaS API without validation.

questions.explanation:
MCP Security Best Practices describes how static client IDs, dynamic client registration, consent cookies, and missing per-client proxy consent can combine to let a malicious client obtain an authorization code without user consent. It calls this the confused deputy problem: a trusted intermediary is tricked into using its identity and permissions contrary to the caller's intended authorization. The proxy must implement per-client consent. It should store approved client_id values per user server-side and check them before starting the SaaS flow. Its consent screen must show the client name, requested scopes, and registered redirect_uri, and redirect_uri validation must use exact string matching. The decisive evidence is [static client ID], [dynamic registration permitted], and [consent cookie].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: A longer cookie lifetime extends the period in which consent is skipped. The problem is missing per-client consent, not excessive consent prompts.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The proxy checks consent per client instead of relying solely on the SaaS cookie, so newly registered clients must receive a consent screen. The tradeoff is implementing a consent store and UI in the proxy.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: The documentation requires exact redirect_uri string comparison without patterns or wildcards. Relaxation increases the possibility of sending authorization codes to unintended destinations.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, confuses related capabilities)**: Token passthrough—accepting tokens not issued for the server and forwarding them unchanged—is prohibited by MCP and can itself cause confused deputy problems.

Further notes: The same structure arises when an agent uses a highly privileged service account for a low-privilege user's request without checking that user's permissions. Use the user's own authority or enforce caller authorization in the tool (see the Serim Logistics case, Q58).

**Sources**: [MCP Security Best Practices › Confused Deputy Problem](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices) (per-client consent, consent-screen requirements, exact redirect_uri matching, prohibition of Token Passthrough) · Verified on the MCP 2026-07-28 specification page

questions.title: Administrator settings that restrict permission requests from consent-phishing apps
questions.prompt: Nuri Insight's IT team is reviewing consent screens shown when employees connect external apps using corporate accounts. Recently an external app with a name similar to a popular meeting-notes app requested permission to read and send email and access files, and an employee approved it. The employee's password was not leaked, and login was legitimate. Legitimate business apps must remain usable, and review of new apps may occur asynchronously during business days. Which measure is most appropriate?

options.text: Enforce MFA for all employees and strengthen password policy.
Ban all external-app connections and have IT build every needed app itself.

Limit direct employee consent to internally developed apps or verified publishers' apps that request low-risk permissions. Route other requests through administrator review and approval, and regularly review approved apps and permissions.
Train employees to read consent screens carefully while leaving consent settings unchanged.

questions.explanation:
OAuth Consent Phishing tricks users into legitimately granting permissions to malicious apps instead of stealing passwords. Hosting on a legitimate identity platform can make users feel safe approving an app. Microsoft recommends limiting user consent to internally developed apps or apps from verified publishers and selected low-risk permissions, enabling administrator review of consent requests, and regularly auditing granted apps and permissions. Even verified-publisher apps require reviewing the consent screen. The decisive evidence is [the employee approved], [no password leak], and [legitimate business apps must remain usable].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, confuses related capabilities)**: MFA addresses credential compromise. Here a legitimately signed-in employee voluntarily granted permissions, so MFA does not address the attack.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, overengineering)**: Blocking every connection also prevents legitimate business apps, violating requirements. Criteria that distinguish risky requests are more appropriate.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Restricting direct consent to trusted apps and low-risk permissions while reviewing other requests preserves business continuity and control. The tradeoff is administrator workload reviewing requests.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Training is supplementary rather than an enforced control. Unchanged settings allow the same approval again and depend solely on human vigilance.

Further notes: If consent has already been granted to a malicious app, inspect and revoke its permissions and investigate mail and file access performed under them.

**Sources**: [Protect against consent phishing (Microsoft Learn)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/enterprise-apps/protect-against-consent-phishing) (definition, restrictive user-consent settings, publisher verification, permission auditing) · The concept applies generally to OAuth 2.0 consent (general knowledge)

questions.title: Preventing internal-network access through a URL-fetching tool
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Accounting built an agent that summarizes web pages at employee-supplied URLs. Its fetch_url(url) tool is a custom client tool running on an application server in a cloud VM, where the server directly requests the URL chosen by the model. The same VM can access an internal administration console and the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254. Security review identifies server-side request forgery (SSRF) risk. The conditions are:

- Employees request summaries of arbitrary public websites, so a domain allowlist is not feasible.
- Implement within this quarter.

Which design most appropriately reduces the risk?

options.text: Specify "do not fetch internal or metadata addresses" in the system prompt and periodically evaluate whether the model follows it.
Place a regex check before the tool that rejects URL strings beginning with localhost, 10., 192.168., or 169.254.
Allow fetching only domains on a list of sites employees frequently use, rejecting all other URLs.

Execute fetching in an environment separated from the application server, allowing outbound traffic only through an egress proxy that blocks private, loopback, and link-local ranges. Validate the resolved IP and connect only to that IP. Disable automatic redirects and validate redirect destinations the same way. Configure metadata access to require session tokens.

questions.explanation:
SSRF occurs when an application sends requests on an attacker's behalf to attacker-chosen addresses, reaching protected targets such as internal networks or cloud metadata. OWASP notes that denylists are easily bypassed through alternative address representations or parser differences, and domain allowlists alone do not prevent DNS rebinding; validate the resolved IP and connect only to it. It recommends disabling redirect following, blocking prohibited calls at the network layer, and protecting metadata with modern mechanisms such as AWS IMDSv2. MCP Security Best Practices likewise recommends blocking private and link-local ranges, validating redirect destinations, and using egress proxies. The decisive evidence is [arbitrary public websites], [server directly requests model-chosen URLs], and [metadata address is accessible].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Model instruction-following is nondeterministic, and successful injection can override the instruction. This is not server-enforced control.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: String denylists can be bypassed with alternate address formats, domains resolving to internal IPs, or redirects. OWASP also treats denylists as a last resort.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: Allowlists are best when destinations are predetermined, but here arbitrary public sites must be accessible, so this fails the requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Network boundaries, IP validation, redirect revalidation, and metadata protection provide overlapping defenses so internal access remains blocked if one layer fails. The tradeoff is operating an egress proxy and a separate execution environment.

Further notes: The fetched page body is itself an indirect-injection input. This design restricts request destinations but does not block instructions in content. Combine it with input separation and tool-permission limits (see Q01).

**Sources**: [OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) (prefer allowlists, validate resolved IPs, disable redirects, network separation, metadata protection) · [MCP Security Best Practices › Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/security_best_practices)

questions.title: Matching sensitive-data protection methods to requirements
questions.prompt: Choose the appropriate protection method on the right for each of three points where card numbers pass through Hanul Fintech's customer-support system. Two options on the right are unused.

options.text: Redaction
Data Masking
DLP
Format-preserving encryption reversible with a key
Shorter log-retention periods

items.text: Remove card numbers from customer inquiries before sending them to an external model API. They are unnecessary for the response, and the original values never need to be restored.
Display card numbers on the support-agent screen with only the last four digits visible for identity verification and all other digits replaced by fixed characters.
If employees attempt to send content matching card-number patterns outside through corporate messaging, email, or file uploads, detect it through policy rules and warn or block the transfer.

questions.explanation:
All three methods protect sensitive information but differ in operation and application. Google Sensitive Data Protection distinguishes Redaction, removing a value, from character masking, replacing a specified number of characters with a fixed character to obscure all or part of a string. Removed values cannot be restored. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) is not a transformation method; it uses policy to detect, warn about, or block sensitive data leaving an organization. The decisive evidence is [no restoration needed], [show only the last four digits], and [detect and block through policy rules].

| Number | Answer | Key phrase |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | {{option:a}}. Redaction | [remove], [no need to restore]. The objective is to remove the value. |
| 2 | {{option:b}}. Data Masking | [only the last four digits, fixed characters for the rest]. It hides the value while retaining part. |
| 3 | {{option:c}}. DLP | [detect through policy rules, warn or block]. It controls outbound data paths. |

- **{{option:d}}. Format-preserving encryption (Unused)**: This transformation is reversible with a key. None of the situations requires restoration; situation 1 instead calls for irreversible removal.
- **{{option:e}}. Shorter log-retention periods (Unused)**: This reduces how long stored logs remain, addressing a different issue from removal before model transmission, screen display, or blocking external transfers.

Further notes: Each method acts at a different point, so no single one covers every path. Combine removal at model input, masking on screens, and DLP on outbound paths (see Q40 for Model Armor personal-data handling).

**Sources**: [Sensitive Data Protection › Transformations reference](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/transformations-reference) (definitions of redaction and character masking) · [Sensitive Data Protection overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/sensitive-data-protection-overview) (formerly Cloud DLP; transformations such as masking and deletion) · The general concept of DLP is general knowledge

questions.title: Limiting uploaded files’ API-accessible lifetime to 24 hours
questions.prompt: Hanbit's customer-support document-analysis wrapper uploads images of customer identity documents to OpenAI Files API, Claude Files API, or Gemini Files API depending on the model used. It deletes them after analysis, but a process failure can skip deletion. Policy states: "Customer documents must not remain API-accessible for more than 24 hours," even if deletion is skipped because of a failure. After checking each platform's file lifetime, the security team must choose the most appropriate design.

options.text: For all three platforms, implement only immediate use after upload and deletion after analysis, with no separate expiration setting.
Set OpenAI expires_after to 86400 seconds and Claude expires_in_seconds to 86400, and rely on Gemini's automatic deletion.

Upload with OpenAI expires_after and Claude expires_in_seconds set to no more than 24 hours. Record Gemini upload times and have a cleanup job delete files that exceed 24 hours. For all three platforms, delete immediately after analysis on the normal path.
Set OpenAI and Claude expiration to 300 seconds (five minutes), then complete analysis; rely on Gemini's automatic deletion.

questions.explanation:
File-storage lifetimes vary by platform, and without explicit settings the defaults apply. OpenAI's upload documentation permits expires_after seconds from 3600 (one hour) to 2592000 (30 days). Files with purpose batch expire after 30 days by default, while other purposes remain until manually deleted. Claude Files API documentation states that files remain until deleted or expires_at is reached, and expiration can only be enabled at upload through expires_in_seconds (3600–7776000 seconds). Gemini Files API documents automatic deletion after 48 hours and supports manual deletion. The decisive evidence is [within 24 hours] and [failures that skip deletion].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Relying only on deletion can leave OpenAI and Claude files until manually deleted after a failure, violating the requirement to remain compliant even when deletion is skipped.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Gemini's 48-hour automatic deletion exceeds the 24-hour cap. Skipped deletion can leave files for up to 48 hours.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Platforms supporting expiration receive a maximum 24-hour lifetime at upload, while Gemini's 48-hour automatic deletion is supplemented by a cleanup job enforcing the cap. The tradeoff is operating Gemini cleanup and upload-time records.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: The minimum expiration for both OpenAI and Claude is 3600 seconds (one hour), so 300 seconds is not allowed.

Further notes: Claude Files API describes expiration as a lifecycle feature rather than a guaranteed deletion control. After expiration, content is no longer API-accessible but may be retained longer for safety review. For strict retention requirements, separately check ZDR eligibility (see Q60).

**Sources**: [OpenAI API reference › Files › Create file](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/files/methods/create) (expires_after range and purpose-specific default lifetimes) · [Files API (Claude)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files) (File lifetime and persistence, Expiration) · [Files API (Gemini)](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/files) ("Files are automatically deleted after 48 hours")

questions.title: Interpreting detection and containment metrics and distinguishing containment from root-cause fixes
questions.prompt:
Mirae Trading's security team recorded timestamps for three agent-injection incidents last quarter. It defines MTTD as the average time from incident occurrence to detection and MTTR as the average from detection to impact limitation (completion of initial containment). Root-cause-fix deployment is tracked separately, not included in MTTR.

| Incident | Occurrence → Detection | Detection → Impact limitation | Impact-limiting action | Root-cause fix deployed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 40 minutes | 30 minutes | Temporarily disable email-sending tool | 5 days later (recipient allowlist) |
| 2 | 20 minutes | 40 minutes | Exclude one contaminated document from retrieval | 3 days later (source verification at document ingestion) |
| 3 | 60 minutes | 20 minutes | Require human approval for tools | 7 days later (reduced tool permissions) |

Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: MTTD is 30 minutes and MTTR is 40 minutes. All impact-limiting actions are mitigation.
MTTD is 40 minutes and MTTR is 30 minutes. Impact-limiting actions are mitigation and root-cause fixes are remediation, so the latter is tracked separately rather than as MTTR.
MTTD is 40 minutes and MTTR is five days. Average time until the root-cause fix is MTTR.
MTTD is 40 minutes and MTTR is 30 minutes. Impact-limiting actions are remediation and root-cause fixes are mitigation.

questions.explanation:
Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) measures occurrence to detection. MTTR averages an organization-defined interval, here detection to completed impact limitation. The R can mean recover, respond, or resolve depending on the organization, so define the metric before use. MTTD = (40+20+60)/3 = 40 minutes; MTTR = (30+40+20)/3 = 30 minutes. Disabling tools, excluding documents, and adding approval first prevent further harm and are mitigation. Allowlists, source verification, and permission reduction remove causes and are remediation. The decisive evidence is the stated metric definitions and the table's last two columns.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: It swaps the values: MTTD is 40 minutes and MTTR 30 minutes.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Both values and the terminology are correct.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, factual error)**: This team defines MTTR as detection to impact limitation and tracks root-cause fixes separately. Five days is average time to remediation, not MTTR.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, confuses related capabilities)**: The numbers are correct, but the terms are reversed. Initial impact limitation is mitigation; fixing the cause is remediation.

Further notes: Improve detection rules and monitoring to reduce MTTD, and preapproved containment procedures (playbooks) to reduce MTTR (see SES-N13).

**Sources**: General knowledge (incident-response metrics and terminology; MTTR is defined in the question because organizational definitions vary) · [NIST Glossary › incident](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/incident) (incident definition)

questions.title: Prioritizing responses to three alerts
questions.prompt:
Prioritizing responses to three alerts

Considering [Incident situation] and [Requirement 1], which response order is most appropriate for the on-call responder?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Mirae Trading is a distributor operating an agent that assists internal procurement. Its security team has four members, with one on-call responder on weekday nights and weekends.

[Existing environment] The agent has purchase-request lookup (lookup_order), supplier email (send_mail), and internal wiki search tools. Last quarter, the on-call engineer delayed disabling send_mail by 50 minutes while awaiting team-lead approval. Different responders followed different sequences, and some evidence logs were overwritten. There is currently no documented response procedure.

[Incident situation] At 18:10 on Friday, three alerts arrive simultaneously.

- (a) send_mail has sent three messages with purchase specifications attached to recipients at an unfamiliar external domain. Calls are continuing.
- (b) Hundreds of agent-bypass attempts have arrived from one external IP over 40 minutes. Input checks rejected them all; no tool calls occurred.
- (c) An external scanner found a model API key for an internal translation-assistance service in a public repository. It has a limit separate from the organizational limit, and usage over the past hour is normal.

[Requirement 1 — Priority] The on-call responder can handle only one item at a time, so prioritize actual ongoing impact or a high likelihood of substantial impact.

[Requirement 2 — Preparation for recurrence] Document response procedures to prevent last quarter's delays and evidence damage recurring. A single on-call responder must be able to follow them at night without discretionary judgment.
questions.explanation:
Triage prioritizes simultaneous alerts based on actual impact, whether harm is ongoing, and exploitability. NIST defines an incident as an event actually or potentially jeopardizing information-system confidentiality, integrity, or availability, but alerts have different urgency and require prioritization. The decisive evidence is (a)'s [calls are continuing], (c)'s [separate limit and normal usage], and (b)'s [all rejected, no tool calls].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: (a) is active exfiltration with data currently leaving the organization and comes first. (c) exposes valid credentials anyone could use, but no anomalous use is observed and a limit applies, so it comes second. (b) has no impact because defenses already worked and comes last. The tradeoff is a window for exploiting (c) before it is handled. This ordering depends on the separate limit and normal usage; without a limit or with anomalous use, (c) should move up.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Prioritizing alert volume violates [Requirement 1]'s impact criterion. (b) has high volume but no impact.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Handling (c), with no observed exploitation, before active exfiltration (a) allows the leak to continue.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Starting with (a) is correct, but placing already-blocked (b) ahead of exposed valid credentials (c) delays a more exploitable risk.

Further notes: After prioritization, narrow containment for (a), such as temporarily disabling only that tool or requiring human approval, is appropriate (see Q80). See Q81 for handling (c)'s key.

**Sources**: General knowledge (incident triage and prioritization) · [NIST Glossary › incident](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/incident)

questions.prompt:
Contents of a response playbook that prevents delay and evidence damage

Considering last quarter's incident in [Existing environment] and [Requirement 2], which contents are most appropriate for the response playbook?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Mirae Trading is a distributor operating an agent that assists internal procurement. Its security team has four members, with one on-call responder on weekday nights and weekends.

[Existing environment] The agent has purchase-request lookup (lookup_order), supplier email (send_mail), and internal wiki search tools. Last quarter, the on-call engineer delayed disabling send_mail by 50 minutes while awaiting team-lead approval. Different responders followed different sequences, and some evidence logs were overwritten. There is currently no documented response procedure.

[Incident situation] At 18:10 on Friday, three alerts arrive simultaneously.

- (a) send_mail has sent three messages with purchase specifications attached to recipients at an unfamiliar external domain. Calls are continuing.
- (b) Hundreds of agent-bypass attempts have arrived from one external IP over 40 minutes. Input checks rejected them all; no tool calls occurred.
- (c) An external scanner found a model API key for an internal translation-assistance service in a public repository. It has a limit separate from the organizational limit, and usage over the past hour is normal.

[Requirement 1 — Priority] The on-call responder can handle only one item at a time, so prioritize actual ongoing impact or a high likelihood of substantial impact.

[Requirement 2 — Preparation for recurrence] Document response procedures to prevent last quarter's delays and evidence damage recurring. A single on-call responder must be able to follow them at night without discretionary judgment.

options.text: Require team-lead and Legal approval before every containment action and provide detailed contact information and backup approver lists.
Focus on reducing detection time by adding and refining alert rules, reducing false positives, and recording detection timestamps, with only brief response steps.
Detail the root-cause analysis report template, ownership and deadlines for recurrence-prevention tasks, and postincident-review meetings, leaving first response to on-call discretion.

Specify initial containment by incident type, actions on-call staff may perform without prior approval (such as temporarily disabling tools or requiring human approval), subsequent reporting deadlines, evidence to collect before acting, and escalation criteria. Run exercises to verify the playbook can be followed at night.

questions.explanation:
A playbook predetermines who does what and in what order for a particular incident type. Last quarter's problems were not detection but a 50-minute containment delay awaiting approval and evidence overwritten because responders used different sequences. Preventing these requires preauthorized containment scope and authority, evidence-preservation order, and escalation criteria. The response-speed metric is MTTR, defined here as detection to impact limitation. The decisive evidence is [50 minutes awaiting approval, overwritten evidence logs] in [Existing environment] and [follow without discretionary judgment] in [Requirement 2].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect, violates constraints)**: Approval before every containment action recreates the prior delay and can be worse at night when approvers are unavailable.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect, suitable for another situation)**: Reducing detection time improves MTTD and suits alert-quality problems. Here approval waiting caused the delay; brief response steps would again produce inconsistent sequences.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect, confuses related capabilities)**: Root-cause fixes and recurrence prevention belong to remediation. Remediation cannot replace initial mitigation, and discretionary first response risks repeated evidence damage.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Predelegated containment authority removes approval delays, evidence preservation becomes a fixed pre-action step, and exercises verify practical execution. The tradeoff is agreement on delegated scope and recurring training effort.

Further notes: Preapproved actions are generally limited to narrow, reversible measures such as temporarily disabling a tool or requiring approval. High-impact actions such as key revocation or full-service shutdown are separated as escalation cases.

**Sources**: General knowledge (incident-response procedures and playbook structure) · [NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final) (integrating incident response into risk management; detection, response, and recovery activities)
